subtopic: DAY OF MOURNING FOR PERSONS KILLED OR INJURED IN THE WORKPLACE MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to introduce a Private Member's Bill asking that April 28 of every year be designated as a day of mourning in remembrance of persons killed or injured in the workplace.
If this Bill passes, every April 28 will become a day on which Canadians will give recognition to those workers who have been killed, disabled or injured in the workplace or inflicted with an industrial disease. In this way we will set an example of commitment to the issue of health and safety in the workplace.
Our most recent work injury statistics available from Labour Canada indicate that there were 23,213 accident claims made between April 1, 1986 and March 31, 1987. Of these, 12,711 required the worker to take injury leave. This is a staggering number of injuries and demonstrates a clear need for greater emphasis on health and safety in the workplace. It is my sincere hope that the passage of this Bill will assist, through a national day of mourning, to increase action on this matter of life and reduce the danger of death and illness at the workplace.
Motion agreed to, Bill read the first time and ordered to be printed.

speechtext: Has the Department of Fisheries and Oceans completed an assessment of the fisheries resources on the Georges Bank and surrounding area and, if not (a) when will the department complete a resource assessment (ft) will the study include an assessment of the impact or potential risks associated with offshore exploration and development?

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
subsubtopic: ASSESSMENT OF FISHERIES RESOURCES OF GEORGES BANK
speechtext:
(a) The Department of Fisheries and Oceans is involved in an active, ongoing program to monitor resources and conduct analyses of the status of major fisheries resources on Georges Bank. The work includes an annual groundfish survey in the spring, exploratory surveys of adult cod and haddock distributions during the commercial fishery season, exploratory surveys to monitor the resurgence of herring, experimental surveys to study the early life history of juvenile cod and haddock, and larval surveys of herring along the Maine-New Brunswick coast. Analysis includes formal assessments of cod and haddock, which are reviewed by the Canadian Atlantic Fisheries Scientific Advisory committee (CAFSAC), as well as the production of various other documents and publications, e.g. on the early life history of cod, haddock and herring, and the resurgence of the Georges Bank herring and its expected effect on the New Brunswick sardine industry.
(b) The Department has recently completed an assessment of the environmental impacts associated with offshore hydrocarbon development. This was in response to a 1987 request from the Gulf of Maine Advisory Committee (GOMAC) for a technical presentation on the impact of oil exploration activity on Georges Bank. The assessment of the possible environmental impacts of exploratory drilling on Georges Bank fisheries resources provides a general scientific evaluation of the likely environmental impacts of exploratory drilling on Georges Bank as perceived by the Science Sector of DFO's Scotia-Fundy Region at the present time. The assessment was considered by GOMAC at their meeting on February 11, 1988.

subsubtopic: ALLEGED LEAK OF CONFIDENTIAL RESEARCH MATERIAL OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. I wrote you earlier today in connection with articles appearing in The Toronto Star, in the Toronto Globe and Mail and, as I now find, in the Financial Post purporting to deal explicitly with confidential and private research material alleged to be a report of the House of Commons Finance Committee and very seriously making allegations about the contents of that report or draft work being done by the committee.
It is exceptionally difficult for committees to operate, and I have checked to make sure that the members of the committee have been most discreet in keeping issues within the committee and making sure that none of it was released. Nonetheless, it is clear from the articles in the press that somewhere in the course of events, Canadian Press reporters Eric Beauchesne and Gordon McIntosh have obtained a copy or what appears to be a copy of some of the preliminary work for report to the House of Commons.
The problem is that the release of the material in the form in which it was released seriously damages the work of the committee and brings disrepute to the members of the committee who must, if they are to act responsibly as Members of Parliament and work with the respect of the financial community and the financial service industry of Canada, responsibly handle matters with discretion. The banking industry has been very co-operative with the committee by supplying the committee material for its investigation. The headlines covering these articles clearly indicate that somehow the banks have refused to co-operate with the committee.
The unfairness of the matter is such that I believe it ought to be a matter of the privileges of the House. Surely we cannot allow the preliminary work of a committee, when the matter has not been resolved by the committee, to be spread around the countryside as if the committee had come to a decision when it clearly had not. This leaves an impression with the public that somewhere along the line, the members of the committee have made a decision that they have not made. That attacks the very ability of the committee to make a contribution to the people of Canada and to this House.
Sir, if somewhere along the line that practice is not discouraged, then our parliamentary committees will be severely

March 15, 1988
Canadian Multiculturalism Act
damaged and the reputation of Members will be hurt. Therefore, I ask that if you find there is a prima facie case of privilege, that I be allowed to move the appropriate motion.

subsubtopic: ALLEGED LEAK OF CONFIDENTIAL RESEARCH MATERIAL OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I, too, would like to support the point raised by the Chairman of the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs and express my great distress at what has happened and its implications for the working of committees of this Fiouse.
We have seen in the last couple of years some very far-reaching changes in the committee structure and these have depended to a large extent on the ability of Members on all sides of the Fiouse to put aside the possibility of partisan or individual gains and work together constructively for the common good. In that spirit the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs has usually managed to come up with unanimous reports. The Standing Committee on Public Accounts, which I have the honour of chairing, also operates in the very same way with a remarkable degree of trust.
As you know, in times past committee members were not allowed to take research material or preliminary drafts away from the committee room. Because of the fear of preliminary leaks, all work had to be done right there in the committee room. We all know how this weakened the quality of the input. The Chairman of the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs has made a practice of doing what I do in the Standing Committee on Public Accounts, that is, giving members research and confidential background materials as soon as they are available and relying on the discretion of the members and their staffs to handle these materials responsibly and not leak them piecemeal, and not interfere with the integrity of the committee coming to a decision.
I feel there are important principles here that go right to the heart of how Parliament works, how the committee reforms work, and I sincerely hope we will be able to find a solution that guarantees that this will not happen again.

subsubtopic: ALLEGED LEAK OF CONFIDENTIAL RESEARCH MATERIAL OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I also wish to support the comments made by my friend, the Chairman of the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs, and state the obvious. We have had a chance to check with the offices of the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) and the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy) who are members of that committee. They assure me that they did not leak the reports or the information. They have checked with their staffs, and their staffs have not done it either. It is a very serious issue which has been raised by the committee chairman. I do not think anyone suspects any Member of Parliament or their staff, and we wish to do whatever we can to make sure it does not happen again.

The Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn), who is also the distinguished chairperson of the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs, has raised a matter which the chair takes very seriously.

Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson) on behalf of the Official Opposition, and by the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom), on behalf of the NDP. I thank the Hon. Member for Mississauga South for raising the matter, and I thank the Hon. Member for Trinity and the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville for putting this on a completely non-partisan basis.

speakeroldname: Hon. David Crombie (Secretary of State of Canada) moved
speakerposition: Minister responsible for Multiculturalism; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
that Bill C-93, an Act for the preservation and enhancement of multiculturalism in Canada, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Mr. Speaker, first let me say that I am pleased to lead off the debate on second reading of this Bill. I might say that I am also very pleased that, since the introduction of this Bill on December 1, 1987, we have had throughout the country a very impressive response. I think it is fair to say there are very few Bills that come before this House, which are complex and sometimes contentious, that have had such a strong and positive response. The Bill has been well received indeed.
If I can indulge in a little immodesty to make a point, I would quote from the Montreal Gazette'.
... Mr. Crombie is right to aim high. It is easy to be cynical about such ideals as equality, bilingualism and multiculturalism, which are too often betrayed in everyday life. But without the ideals-and the urge to make them real-everyday life would be unlivable.
The Toronto Sun says:
Crombie has a good solution. Instead of entrenching heritage language programs in the most radical way and enshrining divisions in other ways, he'd like to see our histories reflect the reality of how our country was built.
The Toronto Star says:
It's precisely by avoiding the temptation to create a centralized multiculturalism department with huge powers that David Crombie does all Canadians a big favour. Rather than shove ethnic groups into permanent multicultural
March 15, 1988

ghettos, he's content to have all Canadians treated the same when it comes to protecting their basic rights and freedoms.
Johnny Lombardi, Canadian Association of Ethnic Radio Broadcasters, says:
The proposed Act pleases me beyond measure ... I look forward... with deep pleasure to shaking your hand in our mutual and personal celebration of the fruition of a dream which has finally come to pass.
Courier Canadienne says:
At long last a Government is making the effort to recognize the realities of an evolving Canada.
Lou Meloski, National Chairman of the Canadian Multicultural Council says:
It is my belief that Canadians across our country will welcome positively the benefits that accrue from this Act. It is an Act for all Canadians, it is an Act that will bring us social peace and harmony that Canadians strongly believe in.
Lucille Blanchette of the Societe franco-manitobains says:
I support the proposed Bill, which will help the country's multicultural groups as the official languages policy helped anglophone and francophone minorities.
Art Miki, President of the National Association of Japanese Canadians says:
The NAJC greets with enthusiasm the new Canadian Multiculturalism Act... which attempts to recognize minority rights and to protect individuals of all ethnic backgrounds from the injustices experienced by (the Japanese) community in the past.
The Canadian Ukrainian Committee welcomes the Act as a long overdue attempt to recognize the contributions that different groups have made to the Canadian mosaic.
Edith Habzmanski of the Vancouver Multicultural Society says:
It's important for the multicultural community to be officially recognized in legislation in Canada; that there is an official piece of legislation that they can refer to.
George Corn of the Canadian Ethnocultural Council said:
We feel it will be a really good and workable act. We offer to work together with the government and both opposition parties to still improve the act.
Javed Hamid, President of the Canadian Federation of Multicultural Councils said:
We are pleased with the introduction of an Act and are committed to working with you through the stages of debate.
Khaki Aziz from the Committee for Racial Justice says:
The act is a welcome step and I am pleased it mentions the country's racial diversity and promotes racial understanding and tolerance.
I picked the best responses, Madam Speaker, because it is, of course, not a perfect Bill but it is a first-class first step. When this Bill goes to committee, as it will, committee members will have the opportunity to recommend those changes which they think are important. I hope they do their work well and quickly, because the Government and the people who have sent telegrams and letters and made public pronouncements want this Bill passed into law. Whatever
Canadian Multiculturalism Act
differences parliamentarians may have among them should not stand in the way of ensuring that Canada's first multicultural Act is passed in the very near future after it gets out of committee.
I read all of those nice comments about the multicultural Bill because I was impressed with the range and depth of the positive response. Even though people have some differences with specific parts of the Bill, they overwhelmingly support the principles of the Bill. There is a good reason for that, Madam Speaker. It is that this Bill is based on the oldest and strongest ideas that the country has to offer. They may have a new application in a multicultural Bill, but they are very old and important ideas.
These are not ideas about Canada which come from an academic pen. They are ideas about Canada which come from the experience of this country, the experience of the people who live and have lived in this country. It is experience that comes from the history of this country. It is experience that comes from the geography of this country. It is experience that comes from immigration patterns in this country and, sure enough, it is experience that comes from the peculiar, particular, and unique approach to nation-building which Canadians have always been able to forge.
That can be seen when we look at how our leaders, over time, have tried to come to grips with a county diverse in its culture, diverse in its language, diverse in its history, and diverse in its life experiences. Some of the most elegant prose written in either English or French in this country been written by political leaders throughout the ages in this country to describe what they understood to be the basic and fundamental reality of Canada's diversity. Let me cite as an example what I think is one of the most beautiful and often repeated statements by then Prime Minister Wilfrid Laurier 85 years ago. He said:
I have visited in England one of those models of Gothic architecture which the hand of genius, guided by an unerring faith, has molded into a harmonious whole. This cathedral is made of marble, oak and granite.
It is the image of the nation I would like to see Canada become. For here, I want the marble to remain the marble; the granite to remain the granite; and the oak to remain the oak; and out of all of these elements I would build a nation great among the nations of the world.

Madam Speaker, more than 25 years ago, John Diefenbaker, who was Prime Minister at the time, used equally striking images when he said that Canada is not "a melting pot where a number of ingredients are amalgamated, thus destroying their individuality, to produce a new and totally different product. This country is more like a flower garden to which the hardiest and most radiant blossoms from a host of different countries have been transplanted, each maintaining in its new environment the best qualities for which it was loved and cherished in its native country".

March 15, 1988
Canadian Multiculturalism Act

Indeed, most recently in a long line of Prime Ministers who have tried to define what Canadian diversity means, the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said a year ago in Toronto:
Multiculturalism is an affirmation of our commitment that Canadians of all ethnic and racial backgrounds have the right to equal recognition and equal opportunity in this country. Thus multiculturalism lies at the very heart of the idea of Canada, of our sense of country. As with our commitment to official languages, it reflects where we have come from and where we are going.
We also saw that sense of the importance of diversity coming from our own experience during the unity debates of the 1960s and 1970s. Some of us in this Chamber are old enough to remember those. I remember in particular a comment made by Dr. Charles Hobart who at that time was a professor of sociology at the University of Alberta, and an American. He said at that time something which cut through to a lot of us. He said that Canadians are almost "the" multicultural society of the world. He said to us in 1963:
-this is your identity. It is the contribution you as Canadians have to make to the world. The system of multiculturalism has now worked for almost 100 years and you should be missionaries in this ... cause.
I remember as well a speech to which I referred on one other occasion by Senator Paul Yuzyk. That Senator from Manitoba was probably the first parliamentarian to put on record the call for the understanding and declaration of a multicultural Canada. In his maiden speech 23 years ago in the Senate he said:
The Indians and Eskimos have been with us throughout our history; the British group is mutlicultural-English, Scots, Irish, Welsh; and with the setting up of other ethnic groups, which now make up almost a third of the population, Canada has become mutlicultural in fact... In keeping with the ideals of democracy and the spirit of Confederation, Canada should accept and guarantee the principle of the partnership of all peoples who have contributed to her development and progress.
It continued, of course, in the early 1970s. In 1971, Prime Minister Trudeau proclaimed Canada to be officially multicultural with a policy directed toward, he said:
Preserving human rights, developing Canadian identity, strengthening citizenship participation, reinforcing Canadian unity and encouraging cultural diversification within a bilingual framework.
Shortly after he made that speech in the House in 1971, he was joined by the then Leader of the Opposition, Robert Stanfield, who said:
What we want is justice for all Canadians and recognition of the cultural diversity of this country.
It did not stop there. In 1972, the government of the day appointed for the first time a minister responsible for multiculturalism. A year later, in 1973, there was appointed an advisory body to the Minister for Multiculturalism.
In 1977, after a very heated debate with respect to multiculturalism, this country adopted the Canadian Human Rights legislation. In 1982, with the adoption of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms not only the equality clause, Section 15(1), but
Section 27 in particular terms were put in the Charter. Section 27 reads:
This Charter shall be interpreted in a manner consistent with the
preservation and enhancement of the multicultural heritage of Canadians.
In early 1984, the Liberal government of the day, through the parliamentary committee, brought forward the report Equality Now. It was supported by all three political parties and called for urgent action to fulfil the promise of multiculturalism in the Charter. Later in 1984, the Liberal government of the day introduced Bill C-48 but, because of the impending election, the Bill was not concluded. Indeed, I think it is fair to say that people on all sides felt more work was needed to be done.
When the new Government assumed office in 1984, the Prime Minister made a commitment through the Speech from the Throne to review the matter and bring forward a multicultural act. We began that process with the establishment of a parliamentary committee on multiculturalism.
In June, 1987 that Standing Committee on Multiculturalism, chaired by my hon. friend, the Member for Grey- Simcoe (Mr. Mitges), brought forward its report entitled Building the Canadian Mosaic. It also made specific recommendations on the content of Canada's first multiculturalism Bill.
Finally, on December 1, 1987, Bill C-93 was introduced into the House.
I have gone through that long history because Canadians sometimes forget that ideas and events do not happen simply in one morning. They have a background to their development, and I want to ensure that it is clear that this Bill fulfils the promise of that long historic march toward a multicultural Canada. This Bill is true to the spirit and intent of Section 27 of the 1982 Charter of Rights and Freedoms. It provides a legislative base for the multicultural policies of the Government of Canada. It recognizes and declares that multiculturalism is a central feature of Canadian citizenship and of being Canadian. This Bill reinforces the historic right of every Canadian to choose to enjoy, enhance and share his or her heritage.
Finally, this Bill commits the federal Government to promote multiculturalism throughout its departments and agencies and in Canadian society as a whole.
If I asked Members of the House or average Canadians across Canada, indeed people outside Canada, what words they would use to describe Canada, they would have varying views about what Canada means to them. Certainly most of us who participate in public life and attend meetings where people concern themselves with these matters would respond with three words: freedom, stability and opportunity. Indeed, that would be the response of most people who know the reality behind those words.
That is what Canada means to Canadians, once the rhetoric is removed. That is what it means to people around the world
March 15, 1988

who want to live in this country. The combination of freedom, stability and opportunity in a society is very rare in this world. Canada has been able to depend upon freedom, stability and opportunity for generations. While we have not always practised it well, and I have occasionally talked about periods when we have had a shortened sense of the values and traditions of this country, I think we can agree with the Canadian writer who said: "When you visit Canada you visit the peaceable kingdom, the peaceable kingdom of freedom and stability and opportunity".
Canada, certainly more than most other countries, has been able to practise a way of life that gives tangible opportunities to Canadians and those who come here to live. Why? How? 1 believe it is because we have always tried to practise three fundamental principles. Those principles are at the heart of this Bill and at the heart of Canadian citizenship. They are equality, diversity and community.
Some people are cynical about those principles. There are some people-perhaps it is the comfortable and secure-who take it for granted that those principles will produce the freedom, stability and opportunity that we enjoy.
As Secretary of State, I have the opportunity to judge Canada Day posters made by kids across Canada. When I read a cynical editorial or hear people express the view that these principles are silly, I look at those Canada Day posters in which eight, ten and twelve-year old kids describe what they think it means to be Canadian. In their primitive way they describe the principles of equality, diversity and community. We must never stop recognizing those principles because they give us that freedom, stability and opportunity.
Equality is not simply an idea. It is and always has been a burning struggle for people and communities in the desire to make sure that one is not diminished as a person or held back because of colour, race, creed or religion. Those qualities that add up to human dignity are daily struggles. Some of us forget that.
Those of us who have the opportunity to visit groups, either newly arrived or those who have historical traumas with which they have to deal, recognize that at the root, equality is an individual and group struggle which must be dealt with each and every generation. Equality is also a social glue. It keeps us together. It is an integrating force. It allows people in this country to say, "I will make a commitment to social harmony and to the stability of this country because it gives me equality of opportunity". Equality of opportunity gives people the willingness to ensure we keep it together.
One notices most, I suppose, in Citizenship Court ceremonies, that equality comes from Canadian citizenship. People who receive their citizenship understand that they now will have equality of opportunity. They know they have to struggle for it but their citizenship is their passport to do so. That is why equality is something we should not underestimate. It is a
Canadian Multiculturalism Act
powerful principle, not only ideologically but it is clearly practical on the street.
People come to this country and stay to live here because they want to be Canadians. First and foremost they want to be Canadians. I might say that that is one of the reasons I rejected a recommendation of the standing committee with respect to a separate department for multiculturalism and a commissioner.
Some people have said I did not go far enough. They are wrong. I think a separate department and a commissioner is absolutely wrong and against the traditions of this country. I might say, Madam Speaker, that I am not alone. If you look at some of the testimony which has been given you will see that others agree.
The Toronto Star, I think, probably does more in the multicultural field, reaching a larger number of people, than any other news media in the country. I will quote it again:
It's precisely by avoiding the temptation to create a centralized multiculturalism department that David Crombie does all Canadians a big favour. Rather than shove ethnic groups into permanent multicultural ghettos, he's content to have all Canadians the same when it comes to protecting their basic rights and freedoms.
It is not because I did not want to go far enough, it is because I reject the view that we should ghettoize people in this country, bureaucratically. Their rights are the same as Canadians. I rejected the commissioner for the same reason. Multiculturalism in this country, historically, and multiculturalism in this Act, is not the language of command control. It is the language of choice and opportunity. People's rights are going to be guaranteed in this Act not by some special commissioner for multiculturalism but by the commissioner who guarantees the rights and freedoms of all Canadians.
Some people regard diversity as a curse, as a problem with which we have to deal. I do not. Diversity, to me, has always been a blessing, an opportunity, and I would like to try to put some emphasis on that, not on how we have to cope with diversity, nor on how we have to solve a problem. I want to give an excellent example of this. The other night I was reading The Law Society Gazette. In it was an essay on The Scottish Enlightenment of the middle and latter part of the 18th Century. What attracted my eye is that it was written by the Hon. Bertha Wilson, eminent Justice of the Supreme Court of Canada. She was asked to speak in Saskatoon on things which influenced her with respect to her thinking about literature and the law, and how her cultural upbringing affected her particular perspective. I will not read it all. It is a delightful essay on its own for those who have an interest in the relationship between literature and the law. What impressed me was the last paragraph. In preparation for her talk at the University of Saskatchewan she went back to Scotland to refresh her mind.
I have amassed quite a small library as I attempted to update a Scottish education of some forty years ago and it has been a privilege to share this experience with you upon my return home again to Canada.

March 15, 1988
Canadian Multiculturism Act And this is the point:
1 have never quite been able to understand the emotional springs that give rise to the love and pride I hold for both the land of my birth and the country of my adoption, how easy it has been for me to become a Canadian and feel completely at home in both French and English Canada. Perhaps it is because there is a mysterious element of Scottishness in the Canadian psyche itself, as Lord Tweedsmuir...
A former Governor General.
... declared at Winnipeg on St. Andrew's Day 1936: "Canada in one sense is simply Scotland writ large". Certainly it has had a magnetic attraction for the Scot and over the years many have come to build a new life here; and could echo the "je me souviens" of their French compatriots. For like them they also cherished memories of the land they had left behind-in the haunting lines of an anonymous poet of this Golden Age of Scottish culture-
And one can find this sign, by the way, in Cape Breton.
From the lone sheiling of the misty island Mountains divide us, and the waste of seas-
Yet still the blood is strong, the heart is Highland,
And we in dreams behold the Hebrides.
I have a Scottish background so I am attracted to that poem. And 1 can tell you, Madam Speaker, that that sense is not unique to the Scottish community. You will find that sense with the Macedonian community that I was with on Saturday night. You will find that sense in the Chinese communities and in every multicultural community in the whole of this country. People have a need to be proud of their heritage. It tells them about themselves. They have a sense of belonging, a sense of roots that is important to them. They need to know that their background is as important as anyone elses, and equal to it, and brings with it a perspective on being Canadian that others may not have.
If you have a Chinese background, you have a different perspective on being Canadian. You share some things about being Canadian but you have a different perspective. I can well remember a poem by F.R. Scott with respect to E.J. Pratt's poem about the building of the CPR, extolling that great historic event. However, he forgot to mention the contribution of the Chinese community. F.R. Scott wrote in his opening lines: "Where are the Chinese in your poem, Ned? Where are the 30,000 who swung their picks at 40 below?" The same story with respect to the Chinese community could also be repeated about other communities.
It drives me nuts, Madam Speaker, when I hear people ask why they cannot just be Canadian. That shows two things. First, they are really saying, "Why can't they be like me?" Second, they would cut this country off from some of the richest cultural, linguistic and philosophical ore that we can mine.
That is why I would like to conclude by reminding us all that whatever our differences with respect to the Bill, and there will be some, we are involved in no small piece of work. Barbara Ward, a British economist, once said that Canada was the world's first international country. Indeed, this country has earned a reputation over the years through its participation in world affairs, the recently held Commonwealth Conference in
Vancouver, the Sommet de la francophonie de Quebec, the Economic Summit in Toronto this June, and the free trade agreement.
These items have been looked at by people around the world. They also watch us in terms of what we do with respect to human beings, in terms of what we do with respect to human rights and in terms of what we do with respect to multicultur-alism. They know we practise it better than anyone else in the world. They know that the world is multicultural. They know that the world is multilingual. They know that the world is multiracial. This gives us a golden opportunity.
For the last Canada Day celebrations held on July 1, 1987, a teacher from Etobicoke, Ontario, wrote an essay. I do not think anyone in the House can say it any better than she said it. She said:
All Canadians of whatever creed, background or colour have a destiny-a destiny to build a country ... If we can live here in harmony and in peace, if we can all benefit from being Canadian, if we can prove our country to be not only a land of freedom, but a land of justice and hope for those who follow, then the rest of the world will come to ask us our secret. Perhaps that can be a contribution we Canadians can make to civilization and to global survival.
I think she has it right. I hope that when we conclude our discussions with respect to this Bill that we will have it right, too.
Hear, hear!

Madam Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I know that it is not customary, pursuant to our rules, to ask a question of the Minister at this time unless there is unanimous consent of the House to do so. However, because of a recent event which took place and because we have here the man whom I call the protector of multiculturalism, the spokesperson for that aspect of our country, I would like to ask a non-partisan question concerning a recent event dealing with the Sikhs, many of whom I had the honour to meet. I seek through you, Madam Speaker, the unanimous consent of the House to ask the Minister a question.

Agreed.

I thank you. Madam Speaker, and in particular I thank the Minister. I will be participating in this debate, although it will not be today, since its subject matter is something in which I passionately believe. It is something that keeps me here in Ottawa.
As Chairman of the National Liberal Caucus I had an opportunity recently to meet representatives of the World Sikh Organization. I arrived in Winnipeg and I met some people, including taxi drivers. I must say that I found recent comments made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) concerning Sikhs extremely disturbing. Maybe this is not political. Perhaps some of my colleagues may disagree with
March 15, 1988

my taking this opportunity to ask the Minister as the protector of multiculturalism in Canada a question concerning this matter. The Minister was very sincere in his speech. 1 listened with interest to it. I hope that he can make a comment today since there is a disturbance that is growing in Canada.
The Minister knows very well that there are 250,000 Canadians of Sikh origin in Canada. If the Minister would like to comment today or perhaps later I would appreciate it. However, I would like him to understand the seriousness of the feelings at the moment in the Sikh community in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for Multiculturalism; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to be given this opportunity to reply to the Hon. Member. I understand the seriousness of the question and the seriousness of the matter.
First, I do not need to speak with respect to the actions taken by my colleague, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark). His intention was clearly to ensure that people in the conduct of their affairs did not create such a condition whereby they would be giving aid and comfort to those engaged in activities which we would consider not to be appropriate. I think that was his intention. He has dealt with that matter himself.
My responsibilities relate to ensuring that I do what I can within the federal limits and, indeed, even beyond, to help with respect to communities that are being hurt. When I first became Secretary of State, and this is true of my predecessor when he first became Secretary of State, the relationship with the Sikh community had not been going well in official circles. Therefore I embarked on a series of building little bridges, perhaps minor in their way, to see if we could ensure that the Sikh community did not feel isolated, alienated or put into a corner and put down.
I have had experience with those feelings myself. I understand what they do to people. As a result I met with a number of groups over a number of months looking for a way to send a message to the Sikh community that clearly we wanted to make sure that they were not alienated from either this Government or this Parliament. The most important aspect in this respect was the establishment of the Chair of Sikh and Punjabi studies at the University of British Columbia. As you know, Madam Speaker, and as the Hon. Member knows, those Chairs are very important to the community and, indeed, to our knowledge of that particular community.
When I went to the University of British Columbia I participated in a ceremony. There were some good people there. However, there were some people who boycotted the meeting. I found that unfortunate. While there were some who boycotted the meeting there were others who did not. Clearly within this community there are some not looking for a bridge, but that is the nature of our world.
I am sure that the Hon. Member knows that whatever this Secretary of State can do to ensure that the community is in good shape and not isolated from the rest of Canada, the Government and I will do it.
Canadian Multiculturalism Act

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to rise this morning on behalf of the Liberal Party and the Liberal caucus in the House of Commons to respond to the statements made by the Minister with respect to second reading of Bill C-93. I also welcome the opportunity because I believe it offers Parliament the first opportunity, with some degree of detail, to venture into the policy area of multiculturalism.
At the outset I wish to commend the Minister, whom I consider to be a parliamentary friend, the Hon. Member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie), for expressing his thoughts with a significant degree of passion and sensitivity as he brought the House through the long journey that multiculturalism has taken in this country.
While it is valuable to understand how and why an official policy of multiculturalism came to be, and while it is a productive exercise to trace the evolution of different multicultural programs and initiatives through the years, as the Minister did moments ago, I believe that the centre-piece of our thoughts and deliberations must be clearly directed toward the future, to finding effective solutions to the fundamental questions posed by Canadians across the land, and to finding remedies to the undignified experiences faced by all too many Canadians.
I believe that multiculturalism has reached an important watershed in Canada. After having existed as an official policy statement of federal Governments for close to 20 years, and after having helped shaped this country unofficially long before that, it is in need of a thorough and refreshing review similar to the efforts now taking place with respect to our official languages legislation. Our policy of multiculturalism requires a rejuvenation of energy and thought, not merely for the sake of change, but for the sake of ensuring relevancy and effectiveness. If our multiculturalism programs are not adequately addressing the contemporary aspirations and dilemmas of citizens, they will rapidly become irrelevant, and irrelevance will only breed impotency.

If we want this policy to stand up to the test of time, and I know we all do, this Parliament must be the architect of the second phase of multiculturalism. It must provide a broader and more far-sighted vision that will draw its strength from the grass roots and be accepted by a new generation of Canadians, wherever they happen to be. It would be a demonstration of leadership that would reflect their conviction that a policy is never an end in itself but, by its very nature, a challenge that is constantly renewed and which demands unceasing effort and dedication.

For many the thought of reform can be threatening, while for others, change signals an admission that the ways of the past were wrong. However, for Liberals reform and change are

March 15, 1988
Canadian Multiculturalism Act
the life-blood which invigorate the body and soul of any enterprise. We believe that the future does not belong to those who are content with today, to those who are apathetic toward common every day problems, to those who are timid in the face of new and bold ideas, and to those who are unwilling to take the necessary risks toward bettering people's lives. After all, Plato reminded us all that a life without criticism is not a life worth living.
I recognize a sense of comradeship with respect to the development of our multicultural policy and heritage. This spirit was certainly reached in the Standing Committee on Multiculturalism. I congratulate and commend the Hon. Member for Grey-Simcoe (Mr. Mitges), who is presently taking the chair, for striking that non-partisan atmosphere and developing that rapport. We must compare that attitude to the record of the present administration. Despite having made 46 specific promises in relation to the federal multicultural policy during the last election, to a certain degree the Government has opted for the status quo and for inaction as opposed to action. Not only has it failed to act on its electoral commitments given to Canadians, but to a certain degree it has also been unable to recognize or define that second phase to which I alluded earlier.
In fact, beyond inheriting an infrastructure created and nurtured by former Governments, basically the Mulroney Government has done very little in the area of multiculturalism policy. There have been no new major-and I underline the word "major"-programs initiated; budgets have dwindled miserably; and the Government's over-reactionary refugee legislation has only served to set back race relations for some time. Indeed, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) is fond of utilizing the theme of multiculturalism. It is a favourite subject during the summer picnic circuit in cities across the nation. But what happens to that rhetoric when the Prime Minister returns to the corridors of power in Ottawa? Where does multiculturalism fit into the Government's agenda of priorities for this country and for Canadians?
During the past three and a half years the Government has strived to find someone within its ranks who understands and appreciates the demands and the aspirations of that portfolio. This is evidenced by the rotating door part-time multiculturalism Ministers who have come and gone. Moreover, it was not until December that the present Minister, for whom I have a great deal of respect, by introducing this Bill that we are now debating, moved on a matter of any innovative significance. However, the Minister did so, I believe, grudgingly. When he initially assumed the portfolio for multiculturalism, he was opposed to the concept of a separate multiculturalism Bill and preferred to incorporate the sense of that initiative into a Citizenship Act.
From my point of view, I believe that the Minister and the Government altered their course and that thinking, following protests from communities across the country with respect to incorporating the sense of a multiculturalism Bill into a more global citizenship Bill, and also because they came to realize
that the Standing Committee on Multiculturalism was about to table a unanimous committee report predicated on a separate comprehensive multiculturalism Act.
Therefore, if one takes it at face value, the impetus for that Bill was not an original or voluntary initiative designed to meet a real need. Instead, it was a Government that, to a certain degree, was embarrassed into a reactionary and reluctant policy response.

Do not misunderstand me. Creating a legislative framework for a policy on multiculturalism is indeed a welcome initiative. Nevertheless, I say the Bill must also be judged in terms of the quality and substance of the provisions it contains and the extent to which it genuinely promotes multiculturalism across this country.
Unfortunately, the Bill is unlikely to live up to its promises. It has been strongly criticized by many organizations across Canada. In fact, after reading the Bill, one is left with the uncomfortable feeling that it only contains some very general principles and objectives.
The authors of Bill C-93 have refused to get into any detail. They have carefully avoided using specific, definite terms, preferring to hide behind words like: should, may, facilitate, encourage, and so forth.
This is not only my conclusion. While I appreciate the process and the initiative of introducing a Bill, we also need to judge the Bill, not by the mere introduction, because that would make every piece of legislation in this House extremely perfect legislation, but also by the substance and the contents of it. When I made those remarks they were not only remarks of an opposition critic but remarks rooted in the comments made by a number of organizations and individuals.
The Minister, in his opening address, made reference to a number of comments made legitimately, quite rightly as is their right, by groups and individuals. I believe to a certain degree we can stand up and perhaps read each other's quotes. To a certain degree that might be valuable and it might not.
I would like to provide for the House other quotations, the other side that Canadians are drawing from this Bill. Mr. Lewis Chan from the Canadian Ethnocultural Council described the Bill as "a symbol without substance".
The Ottawa Citizen wrote:
An empty promise on multiculturalism ... it's a mish-mash of circle squaring ambiguity and clumsy opportunism.
The Globe and Mail wrote:
-multiculturalism Bill gets cool welcome.
The Vancouver Sun wrote:
Ethnic Bill called symbol over substance.
March 15, 1988

Dr. Ubali, Commissioner of the Canadian Human Rights Commission said:
The proposed Multiculturalism Act changes nothing. It is not historic as the Minister calls it. It is purely symbolic. It is old wine in a new bottle.
Daniel Iannuzzi, President of Multilingual Television said:
What we need is the recognition that multiculturalism is an integral part of Canadian society ... the Bill does not allow for such an interpretation.
The Canadian Multiculturalism Press Federation said:
By implementing only one of the major recommendations of the report, the Government is offering Canadians virtually nothing new from the policy established by Trudeau in 1971.
The Hellenic-Canadian Federation of Ontario said:
We are profoundly disappointed by the Government's recent draft legislation on multiculturalism. We are displeased by this action of the federal Government, which undermined the work of the committee, and amounts to nothing more than window dressing. Indeed, it simply reiterates what exists in federal practices.
Unfortunately, there is nothing in the recent draft legislation on multiculturalism of substance for the people of this country.
Therefore, the Bill is primarily satisfied in talking and in dreaming about ideal principles rather than establishing an Act through an enforcement mechanism which would make an honest attempt to ensure that these principles become reality.
Finally, the Government drafted this Bill in complete isolation, and stubbornly refused to draw strength and vision from the recent unanimous standing committee report. It cowardly ignored the all-Party recommendations and, as such, the presentation of this Bill is a missed opportunity, a missed opportunity because the Government neglected to take full advantage of the political green light offered by all three federal political Parties and of the growing consensus within the Canadian community which had advocated significant and comprehensive reform. Thus while the process of introducing a multiculturalism Bill is in itself valuable, the actual Bill in its specific is a mediocre attempt at the very best. The Bill merely confirms the status quo and legislates in 1988 goals and values that were born in the 1960s and 1970s.
For the Conservative Party, the future of multiculturalism is clearly in the past. We as a Parliament, as a country, have a choice. We can either choose to embrace the Tory recipe for multiculturalism or we can build and update a policy that will meet present day circumstances and challenges, and articulate and inspire a vision of things to come.
For the Fiberal Party, the choice is clear and unmistakable. We believe that through such a Bill we, as a Parliament, should not have any hesitation in declaring the policy of multiculturalism is an important national building block, a cornerstone of our Canadian society. Therefore, we should pioneer programs and reforms that reflect their sincerity and the attitude of that belief. This Bill does not do that. This Bill does not accomplish or reflect the sincerity of that statement.
Why, Madam Speaker, why does the Bill tremble about confronting the issues? Why did it not address the matters of a
Canadian Multiculturalism Act
full-time senior Minister for multiculturalism and create a separate line ministry which would do justice to the dreams articulated in all of our speeches as we go across the country?
In rejecting the committee's recommendation for a separate department, the Minister used, as he did today, the statement that he does not want to ghettoize people, that he does not want to ghettoize multiculturalism. If that separate line department is ghettoized, how would the Minister describe and characterize the directorate as it stands today? Why a ghetto when we tried to bring all the structures and programs of the federal Government under one more effective roof? Why a ghetto when we took some of the moneys already existing, not necessarily all new money, but existing moneys from departments and fused them together under this new ministry? Why a ghetto when we would be adding political muscle to the Minister of the day and to the Deputy Minister that would allow them to compete for resources and attention on an even level rather than as a poor, more insignificant sister of government? Why a ghetto when the fusion of these new forces would enable a far superior, a farther reaching and more effective outreach program and delivery to Canadians? Why a ghetto when it would have brought the Canada Council under this separate line ministry so as to avoid the present situation as it stands today?
For instance, if you are an author and wish to write about your roots and your country's heritage and your name happens to be Atwood, you go to Canada Council, get your funding and write your book. But if you happen to have a last name that is Diciccio or Defrancesco and you go to Canada Council, Canada Council will reroute you to the multiculturalism directorate. There the directorate will tell you that they do not have enough funding. If we try to stop that practice, and it exists, why are we calling that a ghetto?
Why a ghetto when this significant change in bureaucratic alignment would signal the federal Government's higher priority for multiculturalism to the Canadian public? Why a ghetto when this new alignment would not preclude this Minister or any other Minister from advocating a multiculturalism policy with all departments and all colleagues in Cabinet? Why a ghetto when this separate line ministry can be seen as a transitional step toward having one day in this country one department of culture, not a department of communications and culture, while at the same time having a department of muliculturalism, but one department that would reflect Canadian culture which is clearly multiculturalism?
That step is not politically simply, nor easy. Rhetoric alone will not achieve it, nor will giant leaps of faith that land nowhere. For me and my Party, a separate-line Ministry represents one significant, positive, sure step toward achieving that ultimate goal.
When the Minister calls that proposal one that would create a ghetto, Canadians ask themselves who really is advocating

March! 5, 1988
Canadian Multiculturalism Act
that ghetto. They ask who ghettoizes multiculturalism, those who do not do very much and want to leave it where it is or those who say let us have a greater breadth of vision, let us be a little bolder and let us change.
Again, that is not something I am saying for my own satisfaction. It is rooted in the words of organizations and individuals who spoke passionately and at great length about this concept of a separate-line ministry.
The Canadian Hellenic Congress said:
We are disappointed however that the Honourable David Crombie has rejected the idea of a new Department of Multiculturalism... the current treatment of multiculturalism policies, within the Government of Canada is unfocused and underfunded.
We doubt that the passing of the proposed Act in its present form will do much to focus or strengthen such policies.
The Ontario Advisory Council on Multiculturalism and Citizenship said:
The decision not to establish a Ministry of Multiculturalism as it was recommended by your committee is unacceptable and it only demonstrates the lack of leadership commitment for multiculturalism as a fundamental goal for Canada.
Professor Michael Lanphier of York University said:
It is recommended that a new department... become the lead ministry in negotiating an enhanced role for multiculturalism in every department.
Therefore, I must ask myself who is promoting the ghetto, who is actually pushing ideals that would build a higher wall around that ghetto, making it all the more difficult to tear it down.
The Bill was also silent about increasing the $ 1 per year per person budget. It did not talk about having a respectable and capable budget that would sustain the programs and contributions to organizations and activities across Canada. It was silent about increasing the personnel within the Ministry and about establishing a multiculturalism commissioner who would report to and monitor for Parliament the policy status within the Government, the federal civil service and Crown agencies.
Again, the Minister rejected a very key recommendation of the committee. As he mentioned only moments ago, he did this on the rationale that Canada already has a Canadian Human Rights Commission and a multiculturalism committee. The Minister himself said that we do not need a system that commands and controls. That is not what was advocated.
We were not asking for a second human rights commission which would be a reactionary body dealing one on one with individual cases of discrimination. We were after an office for a commissioner, very similar to the Official Languages Commissioner; an office that would in fact be free of political compromises and constraints. We wanted an office that would report on the status of the policies to Parliament, not to the Government and not to a Minister reporting to Parliament by saying that all is well. There are few Ministers of whatever political stripe who will fundamentally and productively criticize a colleague's department.
We should be able to have a report to Parliament that would give us an understanding of where the successes lie and where the warts lie and how we should go about eradicating them. We need an office that would promote the policy of multiculturalism across all Departments in the federal Government. We need an officer who would facilitate between the public and the federal bureaucracy the multiculturalism policy, one who would not be timid, if the Government is, about grappling with the issues.
We need an officer who would ask how the CBC is reflecting multiculturalism policy and if it is doing it well enough or if there is need for vast improvements. We need one who would ask if the Canada Council maintains those standards as well and if the Treasury Board's hiring practices are even and equal among all Canadians of whatever extraction.
That is the kind of commissioner we had envisioned, an instrument to effectively enforce and ensure, day in and day out, that the policies are being carried out, respected and lived up to. What is wrong with that? Surely that is not a kind of ghettoization. Surely that is a forward-looking, forwardthinking investment, not only in the words and principles we should all embrace but in the deeds and actions of the federal Government.
The Bill is silent about increasing the amount of government advertising from all departments in third-language media. It does not talk about recommendations for appointments to the Canadian Multiculturalism Council which advises the Government and the Minister of the day, recommendations which should be obtained from the community so that we would know that that council represents the real aspirations, needs and concerns of the people and percolates them throughout our elected and political institutions.
The Bill did not talk about approving a charitable tax number for national ethnocultural organizations to assist them in fund raising and to decrease their dependency on the Government's stick-and-carrot system. It did not talk about an appropriate number of appointees to boards and commissions or, more importantly, about the quality of appointments to these boards and commissions. The appointments must reflect the realistic composition of a Canada in 1988 and not a Canada in 1888.
These are some of the issues with which the committee grappled. The committee distilled that investment of time into this report. The Bill is deafening in its silence on these issues. It prefers to hide instead behind the generalities and noncommitted language we see throughout the Bill.
As Canada prepares to enter the 1990s, the challenge facing multiculturalism is similar to the challenge that confronted bilingualism in the 1960s. Back then, it was a Liberal Prime Minister and a Liberal Government who invested the necessary political capital into transforming the dreams of a truly bilingual Canada into a reality. Pierre Trudeau did not only talk about official bilingualism, he and his Government moved to make it happen. Pierre Trudeau did not craft a Bill which
March 15, 1988

was couched in colourful yet meaningless language. Instead, he and his Government provided the tools and the mechanisms needed to fulfil those policy objectives. They provided an Official Languages Act, a Commissioner for Official Languages, a permanent and joint official languages standing committee, a viable financial base for government-sponsored programs, a secure bureaucratic structure able to support the linguistic needs of our diverse regions and an understanding, above all, that the policy of official bilingualism was a national one for all Canadians in all regions of Canada.

Without the political will and determination that resulted in the creation of these structures, bilingualism today would be no more than an abstract concept. I agree, there was a political price to pay for this political investment. In the final analysis, however, the risk was worth taking.
The controversy aroused by bilingualism should remind us that success will not come easily. It takes hard work and dedication to succeed. Similarly, if we want multiculturalism to have a vital impact on the character and the affairs of this country, we will need the same political will and similar structures. Madam Speaker, if we want multiculturalism to provide an appropriate and dynamic response to the aspirations of future generations, our Party and this Parliament must be prepared to make the necessary political investment.
We should also find the courage to remind all Canadians that a more vibrant multiculturalism policy will in no way undermine our policy of official bilingualism. A stronger multiculturalism policy will not and should not result in a request for official language status for some third language. While Canada has two official languages, its cultural heritage derives from the multitude of cultures living within our borders. Therefore, we should be advocating a stronger multiculturalism policy which will serve to reinforce and strengthen official bilingualism and breathe new life into the concept that we call Canadianism.
For those reasons the Liberal Party will be demanding, through appropriate amendments in committee, that this Bill be reinforced with meaningful substance. It should not stop at symbolism. It should go beyond that to enhance the status of multiculturalism, not for the benefit of those in this Chamber but for the benefit of people on the streets of this country, whoever they are, from whatever background, regardless of when they came to this country. There is no reason, particularly when we consider the recent all-Party report, why this cannot be done. There is no excuse for missing the opportunity which presents itself to this Parliament and the Government.
For those reasons I am hopeful that the Conservative Government, and particularly the Minister responsible for multiculturalism, will rise to the occasion and join in the consensus in the community to boldly usher in this second
Canadian Multiculturalism Act
phase of multiculturalism, rather than struggling desperately to embrace the past and expecting to be congratulated and commended for doing so.
Canadians deserve better. Those fighting in the multicultural constituencies of our country deserve better. Those young second and third generation Canadians who are of neither English nor French heritage deserve better. Their expectations and definitions of multiculturalism may be radically different from those of their parents. They expect this policy to answer new dilemmas, new questions which were not faced by previous generations in the struggle to build this great nation. Multiculturalism deserves more than simply window-dressing. We are talking about national pride, national sentiment, and the forces which came to be fused together in the building of Canada. We are talking about our national fabric, not necessarily about a policy only but a way of life which distinguishes us from any other country in the world.
To borrow an Olympic analogy, the Bill is merely content with the bronze when many Canadians are encouraging their Government to go for the gold. It is with that thought that I end my contribution at second reading of this Bill. The Minister and Government should not be willing to accept the bronze. They should go beyond that. To borrow a phrase from the Minister, the Bill should not allow this policy to be ghettoized into obscurity. That is the challenge at this stage in our evolution.
Multiculturalism, while it has been a general success story up until now, must change with the times. It must focus on and address new challenges and new problems which are surfacing. Many people, while living in a country of opportunity, do not see that opportunity as readily as some others. Some do not enjoy that level of stability. While we all rejoice in being Canadian, while we can compare ourselves with pride to other parts of the world, that should not prevent us from trying to improve our society so that all Canadians can enjoy the opportunity and stability that the Minister talked about moments ago.
While the Government did not embrace the political green light offered to it by the committee and adopt its recommendations, and it could have adopted many of them because they were the guts of a report which represented the sentiments of Canadians across the country, I am hopeful that at committee stage the Minister and Government will try to come at least half way. 1 hope they will realize that the definition of this Bill is that the future for multiculturalism is in the past, and we must reverse that. We must change the language and the intent. We must make sure there is a way to enforce the eloquent words of the Minister when we have to face the problems which come from a growing country. Canada will continue to need the passion of immigrants to build it bigger and stronger.
We must judge this legislation by its substance, and it is our intention to enhance that substance so that when it returns to this House, Members on all sides can take some pleasure in this

March 15, 1988
Canadian Multiculturalism Act
Parliament having boldly and progressively moved multiculturalism into its second phase. I am hopeful that those sentiments will be shared by the Minister and the Government.

Madam Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to speak for my colleagues in the NDP caucus on Bill C-93, a Bill to preserve and enhance multiculturalism in Canada. This is a historic day for Canada. We are for the first time debating a Bill which speaks of preservation and enhancement of multiculturalism in Canada. In many ways it is rather a late point in our history to be doing that, since the policy of multiculturalism enunciated in 1971 has been in effect for 16 years. All Parties in Parliament committed themselves to that policy and gave firm support to the recognition of the diversity of peoples in this country. They supported the desire of the Government to change our policy in recognition of that fact. One need only look at the Estimates which successive governments have tabled to appreciate how very little was done about the policy statement of 1971. Only very gradually were funds set aside for various purposes of cultural enhancement, community integration, and development of institutions respecting mainstream institutions for the diversity of our country. Even more slowly were the institutional means found to support these efforts.
Even now we have a Minister for Multiculturalism (Mr. Crombie) who carries those responsibilities as well as being Secretary of State. If he has to consult with the powerful Minister he can, presumably, do so within the quietness of his own mind and, as Minister of Multiculturalism, question the Secretary of State as to the advisability of action on multiculturalism.
It has been recognized by others that we spend even now about $25 million a year-less than $1 per Canadian man, woman, and child-in support of a policy which was designed to recognize fundamental realities of this country and change the way in which the federal Government operated and, in time, influence provinces, municipalities, non-governmental organizations and voluntary organizations across the country to respond to the diversity which exists in this country.
Why has there been such slow action? Why do we have in Bill C-93 such limited legislation? Why do we have what can, in the most damning of all phrases, be regarded as an institutionalization of the status qtiol We have taken what was in existence and given it a legislative basis, and that is supposed to be adequate recognition.
My colleague, the Member for York West (Mr. Marchi), has suggested that this is multiculturalism dealing with the past rather than the future. I think that in a certain sense he is right in making that particular observation.
The reason we have so little is because the policy of multiculturalism has still not taken true root in the minds of the Ministers, in the thinking of governments, and in the reality of the Canadian Government. The reason that has not occurred is
that it is still not appreciated how powerful are the forces in this country which militate against the fulfilment of the policy of multiculturalism stated in 1971.
Those who have spoken before me, the Secretary of State in presenting the Bill as vigorously as he is always capable of doing, and my colleague, the Liberal critic and member of the Standing Committee on Multiculturalism, have spoken of various aspects of Canadian history. I think there is good reason, on this topic, to look back with discernment and to speak the truth about the history of this country. It is only when we do those things that we will appreciate how much needs to be done, and understand perhaps with some measure of charity why there has been such limited action toward the policy of multiculturalism.
I think back 100 years and more in Canadian history. I find myself thinking of that notable politician of Quebec, George Cartier. I say "George" advisedly because, of course, he was not "George" as is often thought by those who do not know the man in Canadian history. He was George, named after King George III. He was named after a British monarch because his parents thought that the protection of the French-speaking British subjects in Canada was best found in monarchy. They feared the pressures that might be imposed on them by their neighbours, by the Government of Lower Canada, the Province of Canada later and, of course, when he was himself active in politics he might have feared what could happen within the Dominion of Canada. They thought that to be a good subject of the King was possible. If one were Catholic, if one spoke French, if one led a good and useful life in the St. Lawrence Valley in Canada one was a good subject of the King, one could be distinctive and yet serve well.
We are all, of course, subjects still of the monarch. That view of things, carried over to our day, is what we attempt to encapsulate in the concept of citizenship which we all know is very important to the Secretary of State as his fundamental view of the country.
What happened in the 19th century? What was the reality of which George Cartier's parents were keenly aware? There were powerful forces in this country to Anglicize it. There were powerful forces to create one people which would speak English. One hundred years ago in this Chamber, and out of this Chamber an Ontario Member of Parliament named D'Alton McCarthy set forth to make this country English. In the province in which I was born and grew up, the Province of Manitoba, he had some of his greatest successes. He set out there to end the bilingualism which was constitutionally rooted, as the Supreme Court of Canada has told us not long ago.
In his first success he succeeded in persuading a Manitoba Government to betray promises given to a minority and to destroy a denominational educational system, to create a public school system with no respect for the minority, and to move toward making an English-speaking province. It was in fact in the midst of the Great War, a war still of empires at
March 15, 1988

that point, which was only gradually becoming a war in defence of democracy and individual rights, that the Province of Manitoba chose to end bilingual education, which had continued not only English and French but English and German, English and Ukrainian, and so on, in 1916, and insist that education in Manitoba would be carried on only in the English language.
I expect that I, of Mennonite stock, am one of very few peoples which had members of their community leave this country as cultural and political exiles because they found themselves suppressed here. I have distant relatives living in Chihuahua State in Mexico who left Canada in protest because they had come here thinking they could live as conscientious objectors, practise their religion, and use the German language as well as English. When that was taken from them in 1916 many of them left, and I think that that particular aspect of Manitoban and Canadian history deserves to be remembered.
One of the cultural instruments which Canada used in the late 19th century against the aboriginal peoples was the Indian Act with its prohibition of the sun-dance and the potlatch. That Indian Act was designed to destroy a people. It was designed to tear out of the Canadian nation, to remove from Canadian soil, distinctive cultures. We lived with that for three-quarters of a century. Only in the 1950s and 1960s did we begin to turn around. It is that kind of heritage which we have. It is that from which, in the 1960s, we began to turn about.
I see that it is one o'clock. I shall break off at that point to continue the historical exploration and the political consequences of that after three o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, I rise with much enthusiasm to welcome the Montreal Daily News which today published its inaugural edition. I would like foremost, on this special occasion, to commend the initiative and courage of Pierre Peladeau and the Quebecor family.
