It is quite constructive in our pluralistic society to have an additional vehicle, such as this tabloid, to reflect the vitality of Montrealers, Quebecers, and, in particular, the Anglophone community of Quebec.
Congratulations to the staff of this promising tabloid which should stimulate news reporting competitiveness to satiate our society's strong appetite for accurate and informative reporting and promote further public debate. Welcome to the Montreal Daily News'.

subtopic: CALL FOR PASSAGE OF BILL C-54
CALL FOR PASSAGE OF BILL C-54
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pornography is clearly something that most Canadians believe should not have any place in our society. The Government's pornography Bill, Bill C-54, has resulted in the most popular support that the Department of Justice has received since this government came to office.
The Opposition's continuing filibuster of Government Bills is eating up valuable legislative time that could be used in bringing forward progressive legislation such as Bill C-54. I ask the Opposition to exhibit more responsibility in their debates, and also urge the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnaty-shyn) to bring Bill C-54 to second reading and committee.
The Government should not be deterred by the vocal minority in the country. Clearly an overwhelming majority of Canadians applaud the Minister for this Bill.

Mr. Speaker, only days before the anniversary of the Sharpeville riot, the South African Government has announced that "the Sharpeville Six" will be executed by hanging on Friday, March 18.

March 15, 1988
Despite questionable evidence as to their guilt, it appears these six individuals will pay the supreme penalty for the mass violence which has gripped South Africa in the past few years.
I call on the Canadian Government again to urge clemency for "the Sharpeville Six" and to use its good offices to rally international support to that effect. Prime Minister Botha should grant clemency not simply in the interest of the six accused but in the interest of his country as a whole. Why should he push it toward increased violence and bloodshed? These actions show that the South African Government has rejected all standards of international jurisprudence and has clearly turned its back on world opinion.
I call on the Canadian Government to review its policy in regard to South Africa, to consider new measures, including the total economic sanctions the Prime Minister (Mr. Mul-roney) referred to at the United Nations, to bring pressure on the Government of South Africa to institute meaningful changes in the society of that country.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR MORE ASSISTANCE FROM MINISTER OF FINANCE OF CANADA AND FROM MINISTER OF FINANCE OF QUEBEC
REQUEST FOR MORE ASSISTANCE FROM MINISTER OF FINANCE OF CANADA AND FROM MINISTER OF FINANCE OF QUEBEC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since the use of flow-through shares to finance exploration activity, the mining industry in Abitibi-Temiscamingue, Quebec and across Canada has shown unparalleled new vigour.
Risk financing of exploration activities by means of flowthrough shares has been an ideal mechanism for attracting investors to the natural resources sector, and as a result, the unemployed, prospectors, geologists, geophysicists and engineers have been able to work and contribute their many talents to building up our mining industry. In fact, there is some astonishment about the fact that so many people here are making a success of mining exploration. The answer is that people need a challenge. If you don't have a job, it's hard to show people what you can do.
Mr. Speaker, the mining industry is vital to the well-being of all Canadians, and we want some action by Canada and Quebec's Minister of Finance by the end of April 1988.

Mr. Speaker, what is the cause of present delays in contract
negotiations between the Public Service Alliance and the Government of Canada? Why is it so hard to negotiate new contracts before present contracts expire?
Many public servants are now working under contracts that expired almost a year ago. Many of my constituents are asking themselves these questions.
Since the Government came to power public servants have lost jobs, lost security, lost salaries, parking privileges, collective bargaining rights and more. It is high time the Tory Members of Parliament from the National Capital Region spoke up on behalf of their constituents. It is time to tell the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Mazankowski) to approach the negotiating table with responsible offers so that we can deal with collective bargaining in a prompt and appropriate manner.
The people of the National Capital area working for the federal Government do a very good job by and large. They have a right to work and to be treated decently by the Government.

subtopic: HAMILTON CIVIC AIRPORT-SURVEILLANCE OF AIRCRAFT FLIGHTS URGED
HAMILTON CIVIC AIRPORT-SURVEILLANCE OF AIRCRAFT FLIGHTS URGED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to update the House on the continuing progress, and a couple of problems, at the Hamilton Civic Airport. In recent days I have talked individually with Hamilton-Wentworth Regional Chairman Bill Sears, Glanbrook Mayor Helen Bell, Ancaster Mayor Bob Wade, Hamilton Mayor Bob Morrow, along with Regional Councillor Ann Sloat, and a delegation of concerned constituents on the Mountain.
We all agreed on two things. First, we want to see the greatest possible development of Hamilton's airport. Indeed, Pan Am Express makes its official debut at Mount Hope on Thursday. Second, we agreed that we should be doing everything we can to minimize the disruption of the lifestyles of the people I have the honour to represent.
I, therefore, urge the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) to institute a 24-hour monitoring surveillance, or a much higher security profile, because we need to know who and what is flying into Hamilton, when, and how low. We need an improved flight path to lessen the noise impact.
I want publicly to thank the Minister of Transport for his continuing interest and co-operation in promoting the viability of Hamilton's growing international airport.
March 15, 1988

subtopic: SUPREME COURT DECISION-NEED FOR PROTECTION OF UNBORN CHILDREN
SUPREME COURT DECISION-NEED FOR PROTECTION OF UNBORN CHILDREN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since the Supreme Court ruling struck down the abortion law on January 28, 1988, there has been no protection under the law for the future citizens of Canada, the defenceless unborn. I have received letters from an overwhelming number of my constituents, as well as other Canadians, who are calling for full protection of the rights of the foetus.
My belief in the sanctity of human life compels me to share this same view. The protection of the unborn must be the basis for any just society. Without a law governing abortion in this country, lives are at stake. I urge the Government to introduce legislation that will protect the unborn without further delay. There can be no compromise on the protection of human life.
* *
*

maintopic: S. O. 21 TRADE CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-AUTO DUTY REMISSION SYSTEMS
S. O. 21 TRADE CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-AUTO DUTY REMISSION SYSTEMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Conservative Government keeps telling us it has won major gains in its U.S. trade deal. Unfortunately, reality keeps getting in the way. In the trade deal, Chapter 10 deals with the auto industry. It was supposed to have worked out all the problems between our two countries on auto issues, such as duty remission systems and the timetable for dealing with them.
Despite this chapter and despite the fact that the United States is supposed to follow what is in the deal, the Governor of Michigan, James Blanchard, is launching an unfair trade practices case against Canada. He is trying to cut out these duty remissions much faster than the agreement states. The result could be the loss of thousands of jobs in the Canadian auto industry.
Again the United States is trying to have its cake and eat it too. It has pushed Canada into an unfair deal and it is still going after us under unfair trade laws.
* *
*

speakeroldname: Mr. Vincent Della Noce (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State and Minister Responsible for Multicultur-alism):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity today to pay tribute to a figure skating team in my riding, and I am referring to the Canadian champions, now better known as the "Pirouettes de Laval", a team that was unfairly left out as a result of some very biased and personal choices made by a simple person who was responsible for the closing ceremonies committee in Calgary, a Mr. Brian Pockard, who insulted the Quebec figure skating community and amateur sport across this country, a dinosaur who does not understand our Canadian duality, and more specifically, Quebec.
Quebec has suffered more than its fair share of discrimination, Mr. Speaker. I told the skaters, their coaches, the volunteers and their families . . . and speaking on behalf of the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney), the Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport (Mr. Jelinek) and all my colleagues on both sides of the House, I want to express our admiration for their excellent work and urge them to keep on representing our youth and our country the way they have been doing.
Mr. Speaker, a salute to our Canadian champions, the "Pirouettes de Laval," who are with us in the House today. Bravo!

Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words in the House about Canada's excellent performance as a result of policies introduced by this Government.
According to the latest figures released by Statistics Canada, the unemployment rate in this country has dropped to 7.8 per cent, its lowest level in six years. Canada's excellent record for job creation compares more than favourably with West Germany, Ireland, Sweden, Finland, France, Belgium, Denmark and the Netherlands, all members of the OECD.
Since September 1984, 1,213,000 jobs were created, and 653,000 went to women. Women's unemployment dropped from 12 per cent to 8.4 per cent, illustrating our Government's determination to achieve employment equity. Youth unemployment dropped from 18.3 per cent to 12 per cent.
Mr. Speaker, the difference between this Government and the previous one is significant. Under the Conservatives, Canadians are working instead of drawing unemployment insurance benefits!

March 15, 1988

maintopic: S. O. 21 YOUTH OPPOSITION TO CUT-BACKS IN SERVICES FOR POSTSECONDARY STUDENTS
S. O. 21 YOUTH OPPOSITION TO CUT-BACKS IN SERVICES FOR POSTSECONDARY STUDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Director General, Operations, of Canada Employment Centres wrote the following in a memorandum: "Considering the resources allocated for 1988-89, I think it is inevitable that CEC management will question the continued presence of resources on-campus.
The message is clear. Two years ago, we saw a 30 per cent cut in on-campus resources, which severely affected the level of service offered to post-secondary students. Today it has been decided the service will be practically eliminated. Students are getting a raw deal, Mr. Speaker!
No consideration is being given to the needs of the student population, characterized by its homogeneous make-up, the age group to which it belongs and its lack of job experience. College graduates belong to the age group most affected by unemployment. However, instead of dealing with the problem, the Government now wants to eliminate the last vestiges of its placement service. This must be construed as a failure on the part of the Minister of State for Youth (Mr. Charest) and this Government to show any concern about the problems of our youth.
During the past four years, nothing was done for this group, but that was not enough for the Government. It now wants to make severe cuts in the resources of on-campus Canada Employment Centres.
Protests have been heard from the Federation des CEGEP. I support their protests, and all Canadian students will do the same when they realize the extent of these cut-backs.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT LEADER OF THE OFFICIAL OPPOSITION ENLIGHTEN HOUSE WITH HIS KNOWLEDGE OF ISSUE

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: REQUEST THAT LEADER OF THE OFFICIAL OPPOSITION ENLIGHTEN HOUSE WITH HIS KNOWLEDGE OF ISSUE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this government is amending legislation that applies in times of crisis. Over 15 years ago, because of the War Measures Act, Quebecers were victimized by the Liberal Government in power at that time. It is now clear to everyone that the Liberals' extreme intolerance in the form of war measures was unfounded. That fear was visceral and emotional. Quebecers were happily sending other Quebecers to jail.
Because he was involved in that mass imprisonment, the present Liberal Leader (Mr. Turner) should share with this House his knowledge of the issue. The Liberals and their Leader now have the opportunity to apologize to Quebecers. Apologize!

subtopic: CHARTERED BANKS-FEES CHARGED FOR CUSTOMER SERVICES
CHARTERED BANKS-FEES CHARGED FOR CUSTOMER SERVICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian chartered banks have been systematically evading a provision of the Bank Act which requires the express agreement of their customers to the service fees they charge. The chartered banks obtain a blanket acceptance of these from their customers and then charge whatever they think is necessary for their purposes.
For example, the Royal Bank charges $6 for a bank draft in U.S. funds and $8.50 for a cheque in the same U.S. funds. The Civil Service Co-operative Credit Society, in contrast, charges $1 for the bank draft-no charge at all if one is 55 or older- and 35 cents for a cheque.
[ Translation]
The Caisses populaires in Quebec and in French Canada and credit unions all over Canada meet their clients' needs. They use their resources to lend to their community and offer that service without charging outrageous fees.

I would urge Canadians to consider a credit union when they become dissatisfied with their banks.

Mr. Speaker, last week the City of Toronto Council passed a motion calling for changes in the federal criminal justice system so that violent criminals receive more severe sentences and pay for their crimes in full without parole for early release to half-way houses.
During the debate a moderate Councillor with a reputation for common sense, June Rowlands, said:
The Criminal Code has failed society. The pendulum has gone too far; too much concern for the criminal and not enough for the victims or the potential victims.
Councillor Kay Gardner, known for her social conscience, said:
People feel betrayed by officials who allow offenders into our community with little or no supervision.
Them's my feelings exactly, Mr. Speaker. The Government has done great things, but it should take another look at the criminal justice system, and it should do it fast.
March 15, 1988

subtopic: MINORITY LANGUAGE RIGHTS IN PROVINCE OF QUEBEC
MINORITY LANGUAGE RIGHTS IN PROVINCE OF QUEBEC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Official Languages Bill is now in committee. I hope discussion there will reflect a true sense of language justice. As an Anglophone from Quebec I appreciate and support the need to encourage the French language, but should this happen at the expense of other linguistic and cultural expression? Presently we do not have full linguistic expression when bilingual signs are not permitted in Quebec.
Culturally, Quebec's revised Cinema Act is moving to curtail access to English films. Does being a French-speaking province mean that we cannot appreciate other languages? Is this what is meant by achieving social peace at the expense of minority language rights?
If all this makes sense, then opera, theatre, and literature should also be translated for Quebec audiences. While the world revels in the works of Shakespeare, Margaret Laurence, Andrew-Lloyd Webber, or Steven Sondheim, Quebecers are left to bask in our "distinct society".
Quebec will only earn its place in the cultural and democratic world by promoting all films, theatre, literature, and languages; then the French language in this so-called distinct society will be a respected distinction instead of a handicap, and we will demonstrate our respect for rights and freedoms fit for our democratic society, thus promoting social peace.

subsubtopic: SOUTH AFRICA-IMPENDING EXECUTIONS OF "THE SHARPEVILLE SIX"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. Yesterday the Government of South Africa continued its barbaric policies by announcing the execution, this Friday, of "the Sharpeville Six", one black woman, and five black South African men, despite the pleas from all over the world that the sentence be commuted and despite the fact that none of those six participated directly in any murder.
Yesterday the lawyer for those six condemned individuals said that the only hope for them was a plea from Prime Minister Thatcher, from President Reagan, and from Chancellor Kohl.
I would like to ask the Prime Minister, who places a very high priority on the problems in South Africa, if he will contact those three allies and ask them to make this "last
Oral Questions
hope", to send an appeal to the South African Government to save those six lives.

subsubtopic: SOUTH AFRICA-IMPENDING EXECUTIONS OF "THE SHARPEVILLE SIX"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I share the deep outrage and profound dismay of my honourable friend in regard to the announced actions in South Africa. The Canadian Government has already conveyed its very strong views in this regard. We have spoken with allies as well, and would be happy to again.
On behalf of the Government, the Parliament, and the people of Canada, I have sent a personal message to the President of South Africa asking him to suspend the action contemplated by the Government of South Africa, and to reflect very humanely and seriously on the enormity of the action contemplated.
We deeply disapprove of this, and have conveyed our views in this regard directly to the President of South Africa.

speechtext:

East): Mr. Speaker, considering that another 38 people are on death row in South Africa, all having been condemned in similar circumstances to capital punishment for their participation in a demonstration during which somebody was killed, is the Government prepared to support the request made by a number of religious leaders to the effect that the United Nations take immediate action to settle that terrible situation?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REQUEST THAT THE GOVERNMENT SUPPORT CERTAIN RELIGIOUS LEADERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we want to explore every possible means at our disposal that would bring about a change of attitude in the South African government. As the Hon. Member knows full well, the United Nations' Security Council considered taking action against the most recent legislation in South Africa. We want to have direct talks with Mr. Boesak and other opposition leaders to the apartheid regime in South Africa. We intend to pursue all other available means to express Canada's attitude and to encourage the South African government in taking a humanitarian approach in cases such as "Sharpeville Six" and others.

ability to make choices based on a full disclosure of the facts, and that I am certain will occur.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext:

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Crombie that Bill C-93, an Act for the preservation and enhancement of multiculturalism in Canada, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: When the House rose at one o'clock p.m. the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Epp) had the floor.

Mr. Speaker, when I was speaking just before we rose at one o'clock, I was commenting on the shortcomings of Bill C-93. It is a good first half to the whole Bill, but it is only half the Bill we should have. Even though the Government has given us the opportunity of historic debate on a Bill to enhance multiculturalism in Canada, which we are doing on second reading, we do not have the kind of Bill we want. I think the reason for that is to be found in Canadian history.
If we go back a quarter century to the events of the 1960s, we can see how Canadians began to grapple with the forces that had been at work for a century and more to create a nation of one language in which cultures were to be re-made and peoples were to be assimilated into one particular culture. It had taken more than half of this century before Canadians were brought to the position of recognizing that the diversity of this country makes such a policy impossible. It was only because of the explosive events of the 1960s, particularly the unrest that arose in the Province of Quebec, that Canadian Governments came to grips with that truth.
In the work of the Royal Commission on Bilingualism and Biculturalism we had recognition of the fact that the Quebe-cois required a recognition which would force the Government of Canada to change its policies. In 1969 that came in the form of the Official Languages Act. However, it proved to be inadequate.
Even in the work of the Royal Commission on Bilingualism and Biculturalism there was a representative in the form of Dr. J. B. Rudnyckyj who spoke for Ukrainian Canadians, and by extension for all of those in the third reality of Canadian history.
In terms of what was happening in those years we might speak almost of the fourth reality because, after all, there were aboriginal peoples first, then the French and the British, along with the diversity of British peoples, and then all the others who came to Canada. It was at Dr. Rudnyckyj's insistence that it was inadequate for the Government of Canada to establish two official languages and to settle for a policy of biculturalism.
We find in the fourth book of the work of the Royal Commission a transition from biculturalism toward multiculturalism. The result was that famous policy statement in 1971 in which then Prime Minister Trudeau declared:

A policy of multiculturalism within a bilingual framework commends itself to the government as the most suitable means of assuring the cultural freedom of Canadians.

This policy of multiculturalism in a bilingual framework became the position that the Government of Canada supposedly took. All four Parties responded to that in appropriate style. The then Leader of the New Democratic Party, Mr. David Lewis, after indicating his support, declared that this statement of principles would be a mockery and a betrayal of high ideals and objectives unless collectively we provided the funds to make the principles meaningful in the lives of the minorities in Canada and unless we developed programs in consultation with the minorities giving them every opportunity to participate in the development of programs rather than imposing such programs on them.
March 15, 1988

As I said at the outset, the funds that were dedicated to this policy proved to be sadly inadequate. This indicated to what a limited extent the Government actually acted on the policy.
In terms of underscoring the extent to which the policy on multiculturalism brought about a change in the understanding of Canada, in those very same years-1969, the year of the Official Languages Act, through 1971, the year of the multiculturalism policy-the Government was forced to do an about face on its policies regarding aboriginal peoples.
Canadians will remember the White Paper of 1969 which was designed to do away with reserves, to end the collectivities of Indian bands and to offer aboriginal peoples the blessings of individual Canadian citizenship. The outcry that that aroused still reverberates through the halls in which Canadians do politics. The failure of Canadian Governments to respond fully to the assertion of the aboriginal peoples, that they have the right to govern themselves, underscores in still another area the fact that the Government of Canada did not really enthusiastically throw itself into developing a policy of multiculturalism.
Thus we have very limited responses. We can appreciate how limited those responses actually were and how limited the actions of the Government on the multiculturalism statement of 1971 were if we look at the one area of culture and the other area of justice for individuals, of human rights in short, and recognize the failings of the Canadian Government in advancing multiculturalism in these areas.
What happened in the cultural area proved to be very revealing. A department of multiculturalism, which recognized that there was no longer, if there ever had been, an official culture in Canada, was not created. The Government's support for cultural activity had become quite large. If we think of broadcasting, support for scholarship and all the activities which the Department of the Secretary of State would support in these years, we see that the Government did a great deal for culture.
But the significant thing about that was that it remained as diverse, as unco-ordinated and as unrelated to the policy of multiculturalism as one could imagine. In looking at what Governments did in those years one would think that the policy of multiculturalism had never been enunciated and had never been agreed to by all the Parties in Parliament.
What happened in these years culturally, in particular, was that the Department of Communications was created and the Minister of Communications became the culture Minister of the federal Government in all those areas dealing with electronic media, and far beyond that as the years passed. As we now well know from looking at the way in which broadcasting developed in Canada through the 1970s and on into the 1980s, the Minister of Communications behaved as if a policy of multiculturalism had never been expounded. The Minister behaved as if it had never been declared that there was not an official culture in either the English or the French language which the Government of Canada was to support.
Canadian Multiculturalism Act
That is a failing on which the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi) focused in terms of the Canada Council and the multiculturalism sector when it comes to support for writing, for example. The Canada Council will support those who appear to be working in certain mainstream traditions. These are presumably the official cultures of the country. However, when someone whose name is of another origin than British or French, someone who appears to be working in a different culture tradition, the Canada Council is not interested and fobs that person off on the multiculturalism directorate.
That is an indication of the kinds of ghettos of neglect which are the reality of Canada through 16 years and more of the multiculturalism policy. It is simply not acceptable for the Minister to speak of rejecting the recommendation from the committee, our unanimous recommendation from the members of the Standing Committee on Multiculturalism of all three Parties. In fact, five out of seven members of that Committee from the Government caucus were in support of creating a department of multiculturalism. It is simply not acceptable for the Minister to declare that that would ghettoize multiculturalism.
What his comment reflects is all the inadequacy of the attitudes that continued through 1971 and beyond in which the Department of Communications would control within certain directions, and the CRTC would be forced, very slowly and grudgingly, toward recognizing the needs of ethnic broadcasting, and hardly act on them adequately in any kind of national sense, even 16 years after the policy was enunciated. The Canada Council would go about its way inadequately funded, barely able to support those it regards in its province, supporting high culture, supporting those companies which its funding has enabled to become professional but rejecting those it sees as practising the folk arts. It would reject those who are forced to be amateur because they have not been able to garner the support of national and provincial art councils. Those are left outside.
There we have a continuing situation of neglect in the cultural area. There we have the continuing reality of ghettos of neglect which the Minister is quite prepared on the face of the evidence of Bill C-93 to allow to continue. There, on the cultural side, is the refusal to create a department of multiculturalism which would ensure that all of the federal Government's cultural activities would be brought together into one area under one Minister and his deputy and co-ordinated in such a way that the Government was not handling cultures unfairly. There is one of the evidences of shortcomings still in this Bill and through years of policy.
On the other side we have the matter of human rights. As the Secretary of State (Mr. Crombie), the Minister responsible for multiculturalism, pointed out, it was half a dozen years after the multiculturalism policy was enunciated that the Government of Canada and the Parliament of Canada passed the Canadian Human Rights Act establishing a commission to deal with matters of discrimination of all sorts.

March 15, 1988
Canadian Multiculturalism Act
Did the establishment of a commission to deal with discrimination on the basis of gender, of ethnic or racial origin produce genuine fairness for Canadians? The Standing Committee on Multiculturalism considered a report last spring which raised doubts about the affirmative answer to that question. The committee was told five years after the Canadian Human Rights Act had been passed that in the work of the Canadian Human Rights Commission there was a difference in the way in which different types of complaints were handled.
When complaints about discrimination on the basis of gender were brought before the Canadian Human Rights Commission there was a vigorous assault on the situation, if I may use as vigorous a verb as that. There was a careful consideration of the institution within which the person had been employed or against whom this person was complaining, paper was obtained, and systematic approaches were undertaken to decide what this person-presumably a woman, given what we usually expect in the way of gender discrimination- had suffered in relation to discrimination in the workplace or in other ways. The commission had a good deal of success in dealing with those matters.
However, if someone came forward with a complaint of discrimination on the basis of racial origin or ethnic background the commission did not use the same approach. There was not a systematic examination of the institution against which this person was complaining, or the superiors against whom the person was complaining. Instead, the investigators began looking for overt expressions of discrimination. The fact that people are usually sensible enough not to cast aspersions on individuals to their faces, or in the hearing of those who were prepared to testify, left those complainants without satisfaction.
I was compelled to ask the then Chief Commissioner of the Canadian Human Rights Commission whether this difference did not represent, on the part of the Canadian Human Rights Commission itself, systemic discrimination against those who had complaints based on race or ethnic origin. Although the Chief Commissioner rejected that possibility, it was an indication of the extent to which the Canadian Human Rights Commission had failed Canadians on the basis of consideration of 100 and more files in the possession of the Canadian Human Rights Commission.
In both of those areas there is evidence of grave shortcomings in the way in which federal Government institutions responded to the statement of 1971. We recognize that in the spring of 1984, in its last days in office, the Trudeau Government put forward a multiculturalism Bill. It was a very weak Bill. No one would say much for it except that it was an attempt to enunciate some of the principles.
Unfortunately, one cannot say much more than that in regard to the Bill presently before us, Bill C-93. It is the more or less good first half of the type of Bill that we really want. In
considering what is not included in this Bill, I wish to consider some of the important questions which are before us.
After we rose at one o'clock, I chatted for a moment with the Minister outside the Chamber. He stated that he was tempted to call across the floor when I was talking about the aboriginal peoples. Of course, they had their Department. The Minister wished to make the argument that Indian Affairs demonstrated the type of ghettoizing that is his argument for not having a full-fledged department of multiculturalism. That has some truth to it. If one wants to look at how the Canadian Government could seek to destroy cultures and what it could do in the way of perpetrating cultural genocide, one need only go and look at Indian Affairs. I would suggest that that is not the only model that we can have.
The Minister stated that he did not want a department that could command and control. Neither do I. I do not think that anyone would want that. I am anxious about the proposition of more staff and more animateurs in the field to carry out the work of organizing groups and urging them on. That has to be done with care. I think that there are better ways of doing that than enlarging the field staff in the Department of Secretary of State. What is needed is money for organizations, far more than staff.
But the question remains, how can one ensure that the institutions of the federal Government respect the policy? In considering how a department of multiculturalism could ensure that the policy becomes what it should be, the first line of the federal Government's interaction with the communities and with the diversity of cultures would be if such a department were responsible for all the cultural activities of the federal Government. The standing committee looked in that direction with its recommendation that the department and the Minister should become responsible for the Canada Council. That was only a partial solution. It will inevitably arouse debate if the Government takes it up.
What we want is not necessarily for all those institutions to be put into a department. The reality is that those agencies, whether it is the Canada Council, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, Radio-Canada, or other agencies, are at arm's length from the Government. What is wanted is a mechanism by which they can be brought into an acceptance of a policy of multiculturalism, and forced to act upon it. I would suggest that the committee's report goes only part way towards that.
Last spring in considering a minority report forced on me by the refusal of the committee to deal with issues of racism explicitly in a historical section of the report, I was forced into considering those questions with my colleagues and thinking of different ways of doing that. I would suggest to the Minister that what is wanted is a full-fledged Minister of multiculturalism who, because he or she has at least partial supervisory responsibility for all the cultural activities and human rights activities of the Canadian Government, will be recognized as having some real clout in the Government. Given that he or she is a full-fledged Minister with a deputy minister, there is
March 15, 1988

the clout that Government requires in dealing with other departments and with agencies.
As the committee's own tentative suggestion does not, this would recognize, of course, that there are other departments involved. The Department of Communications in its general responsibility for electronic communications is sure to remain in the field. The New Democratic Party's response to multicul-turalism issued at the end of June suggests that there should be a dual reporting relationship in which the Minister of multicul-turalism has a joint responsibility with the Minister of Communications (Miss MacDonald) and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) to receive reports and to pass suggestions on to the cultural agencies. In this manner it would ensure that in every area, whether it is support for native friendship centres, aboriginal programs, or in the areas of the English-speaking culture that CBC and the Canada Council support, or those supported by Radio-Canada and the Canada Council, all of those activities presently in the multiculturalism sector would be carried out in awareness of each other and under the direction of a Minister who has total responsibility. This would end a charade of political multiculturalism.
Because the Trudeau Government refused to follow through, in this holistic way, in changing the institutions of the federal Government, too many people still think in terms of ethnic politics; dinners, banquets, speeches, in which they crave some type of attention. In an election year they get quite a bit of it from the Government, but not much in between.
When the Canadian Ukrainian communities met in a triennial convention a couple of years ago in Winnipeg, and looked for the usual cabinet Minister to address them, they were forced to settle for a private Member. Unfortunately, they were not meeting during an election year, or they would certainly have had the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) there, as he was at the Jerome dinner last Saturday night in Toronto.
In an election year, all kinds of attention is paid to communities. But the reality of the changing institutions, ensuring that the policy of multiculturalism has all cultural and human rights activities related to it, is that this does not happen. It does not happen in this Bill in which the second half dealing with means is practically missing. There is a ministry reestablished by a provision or two, the standard ones, and there is the advisory council which dates back to 1973 given a legislative framework. There is no substantial department, or a Minister with real influence, because of the voice that he or she would have, and responsibility for all of those activities.
We do not have a council that would have the kind of independence required in the matter of the status of women, for example. We have a council that does have independence with staff and research people who are producing reports that can be published and can advance the cause. What have we had for years under Liberal Governments and now for three and a half years under the Conservative Government and the
Canadian Multiculturalism Act
advisory council is bodies that meet occasionally, not frequently enough, large ones, small ones, that meet behind closed doors. They may have a reception occasionally and issue a statement, sometimes not all that well advised, but these bodies are really private bodies for the Minister and are closed to others as far as their deliberations are concerned. That is not the kind of body we want. We need a strong Minister with a good department and we need a council that is a public body. We need a council that is responsive to the communities because it is selected from the communities.
The model developed in Manitoba is the Manitoba Intercultural Council. A council that is largely a chosen body selected by the communities is able to deliberate with all the freedom that that gives it. It is a council with significant funding for the support of multiculturalism and is a far better model than anything that federal Governments since 1973 to the present have come up with. That is the kind of route we should take.
If we had research capacity and a significant budget for that body, we could have funding made available to organizations with much less concern about the politics of the whole thing. It would put support for multicultural organizations and ethnocultural organizations at the same arm's length relationship from Government that now characterize the cultural agencies of the Government and the Canadian Human Rights Commission. That is the kind of model I suggest should be used.
The Minister has rejected a full-fledged department. He has been forced by the Government-he does not make these decisions by himself-to remain the kind of junior or part-time Minister he is now, being primarily occupied with his duties as Secretary of State. There has been debate among organizations and in the communities as to the best way to go. Not everyone is in support of a department. I think that has a good deal to do with the inadequacies of government action for almost a decade and a half now, in fact, back to the early 1970s. If we had had the proper policies, people would be much more prepared, I would suggest, for a department.
The refusal to create a commissionership represents a far more serious failing. There are people who are concerned about large departments and about what government can do. There are, among all of those concerned about advancing a policy, far fewer doubts about a commissioner. It is again one of those things that can arouse jealousies. God forbid that we should. It is the game of divide and conquer that has gone on for very long in this area and in other areas.
People look at the Commissioner of Official Languages, who has been at work since the Official Languages Act authorized the position back in 1969. They look at the Joint Standing Committee on Official Languages and the way in which the committee and the commissioner can work together, if you will. I have been privileged as a member of that joint standing committee to see how it operates and how effective it can be in bringing pressure to bear on the Government. People see that the Commissioner of Official Languages can make a real

March 15, 1988
Canadian Multiculturalism Act
difference. In the refusal of a government to do the same thing for multiculturalism, they recognize the extent to which this is pre-Christmas tinsel. It is symbolism. A gift is supposed to be given, but there is nothing inside. There is no muscle, no power and no protection for people except what a Minister, who is obviously a Minister of the same Government, might actually be able to bring to bear.
If one has doubts about a department, surely one should be prepared to move in the area of the establishment of the position of commissioner who would be able to assist the Standing Committee on Multiculturalism, the one real advance which this Parliament has made and for which this Government deserves thanks. In the establishment of that standing committee, we have some movement in the right direction. But we have the refusal to establish the position of commissioner who would have the means to review what is going on in government, who would have the means to receive complaints, who could comment on the failure of cultural agencies to respect multicultural policies, and who might have taken reports half a dozen years ago in the human rights area from people who thought they were not obtaining justice from the Canadian Human Rights Commission. A commissioner can do his work often behind the scenes, investigating, issuing reports that are confidential to departments initially. If one takes the procedures that are in the Official Languages Act which are now being proposed in Bill C-72, the commissioner could ensure that the Government really respected the words spoken in January, 1971 to which successive governments of Canada have given lip-service.
What is wanted, Madam Speaker, is real action, not just words. We have had a lot of rhetoric. We have in this Bill the first half of a good Bill. But we need much more than that. I see the failure of this Government to propose anything more. This morning's comments from the Secretary of State suggest that there is no readiness to take up the commissionership, which I know remains the key concern of the Canadian Ethnocultural Council which speaks for several dozen organizations across the country. A commissionership is required, and there is the real failure of the Government.
We are left then with the half loaf that we have had all too often from the Government. Maybe we expect it, but I think the Government in the politics of an election year, would not want to concede that anywhere in public. We have the same kind of half loaf we got with Bill C-62, the employment equity Bill, in the first session of this Parliament. The Government accepted some changes to that Bill. They were very minor. In fact, they were so minor that my colleagues in the New Democratic caucus were forced to vote against the Bill at third reading.
In the case of the multiculturalism Bill, that would be a sad fate for the principles that are there. Whatever rearrangements one might want to make in some cases, it is particularly necessary in Clause 3(2) where federal institutions, it is suggested, should do some things rather than following the shell that is common in legislation of this Parliament. There,
particularly, are reasons for suspicion. We look to the Government-presumably the legislative committee, unless the standing committee gets the responsibility, but wherever it is, I expect to be there-to have some sensitivity to the criticisms issued by many people. I have the privilege as a Member of Parliament to articulate them, while others are forced to do so in press conferences elsewhere or statements of one sort or another, but there are lots of criticisms.
The Minister attempted to lay on us the fine words of various correspondents, editorial writers and so forth, but he knows perfectly well that the Bill is regarded as a half measure, a half loaf. If there is any real sensitivity to what is wanted across the country and what is asked for from so many groups-we heard it again in Toronto in public hearings at the beginning of December-I look to the Government to be prepared to do something in addition to the Bill that is being put before us in Bill C-93.
The ethnocultural communities, the multicultural organizations of the country, want a lot more than this, given that they have had to wait sixteen and a half years since the policy was enunciated. It is almost 20 years since the Official Languages Act was passed. These people have waited for a long time to get something. For them to be forced to settle for half measures as they are in this Bill is a tragedy and is an indication of what little progress we have made toward recognizing what the policy of multiculturalism really requires of the federal Government.

speakeroldname: Mr. Vincent Della Noce (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State and Minister Responsible for Multiculturalism):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I also have a few comments to make.
I heard what my two colleagues had to say about the Bill before the House today. Bill C-93, the Canadian Multiculturalism Act, a piece of legislation that is a historic landmark. The purpose of this Bill is to reflect Canada's multicultural and multiracial reality in every aspect of our life as a nation. It requires the Government of Canada to enhance and strengthen the principles of multiculturalism, and it contains a firm government-wide commitment to implement those principles.
Madam Speaker, I was checking my notes just now. This Bill was introduced for first reading on December 1, 1987, and after the question put by the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi), I said that to me it was a great day when Canada tabled its legislation on multiculturalism. I believe Canada was the first country in the world to table this kind of Bill. It was not only a great day for Canada and Canadians of ethnic origin like myself, it was also an historic moment for Canada. As a Canadian of ethnic origin who had the privilege of being here in Canada and becoming a Canadian citizen, I was very proud indeed.
Madam Speaker, I was listening earlier to my two colleagues, the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi) and the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Epp). I
March 15, 1988

must say that what I heard really takes the cake! Their telephone numbers should be changed to read: 992-blahblah-blahblah. Incredible, what I heard here in the House today! We are just starting second reading, and I made a few notes. Unfortunately, I was not in the House to hear the speech by the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi) from start to finish but I caught bits of it here and there.
So I heard his speech, and I think we should not forget it was his Party that tabled a parody of a Bill on multicultural-ism during the last days of the previous Government. Talk about meaningless promises! He criticized this Bill, but the Bill to which he was comparing it, Bill C-48, was vastly inferior. Why, Madam Speaker? First of all, they made a number of comments. In fact, I had the pleasure of sitting with them on the Multiculturalism Committee. The Bill referred to by the Hon. Member for York West, the official critic in the House, did not recognize multiculturalism as a characteristic of our society, while our Bill does. It did not reflect the essential link between multiculturalism and official languages, and ours does. It had no policy for federal institutions, and ours does. It did not provide for a government-wide commitment, and ours does. It is easy to talk but what we need is facts. Their Bill did not provide a mechanism for ministerial and parliamentary responsiblity but ours does. Madam Speaker, their Bill did not recommend creating a department or appointing a commissioner. So why should we bother comparing the two? No, Madam Speaker, Bill C-48 did not recommend creating a department or appointing a commissioner.
Why persist? Why rack one's brains with that, since, either it was no good then or it has been forgotten, and now it has become a priority. There would be a lot to say about that. Therefore, where was the previous Liberal commitment? Maybe the Hon. Member worked on Bill C-48, maybe he devised the whole system in Bill C-48, perhaps he gave some advice to his colleagues or former colleagues. It is a commitment to hollow promises made in the safety of opposition benches. Nothing more! It was quite simply rhetoric.
Earlier today, the Minister summed it up very well. He rose in this House, and I must congratulate my colleague, because he very well expressed what people, ethnic groups, those who built this country have suggested and what they want. They do not want to be ghettoized. They do not want to be caught up in a separate system.
Madam Speaker, we are not any better or worse for having immigrated to Canada. The Minister summed up what this country is all about when he said: This country of privilege . .. and I insist on that, Madam Speaker, because it was a privilege to be accepted in this country. And those who do not recognize that privilege are not good Canadian citizens.
People like myself, immigrants, chose this country for three reasons the Minister very aptly outlined this morning: freedom, stability and opportunity. We, more especially in my community, in my family, used those opportunities and those freedoms, and we are quite proud of that. We have been
Canadian Multiculturalism Act
accepted in this country, and we now realize that it is a very great privilege indeed, and I would urge all those who are new Canadians to enjoy and to appreciate what they have.
Everytime I meet a new Canadian, I remind him that he is not here to claim the rights of his native country, he is here to accept the laws of this country, to enjoy all those privileges- stability and opportunity. Because if people start to claim conditions in their own countries, we will have no time left to deal with this country, the stability in this country.
The multiculturalism policy of Canada will be the responsibility of cabinet Ministers. This should answer many of the questions of my dear colleagues across the way. I know that there has been some suggestion that a separate department of multiculturalism be established. I strongly believe that such an isolated, separate department of multiculturalism would not be in the best interests of the Canadian people.
Let me refer to an article from The Toronto Star, a newspaper which writes its own articles. I do not think the Government tells it what to write. The Toronto Star says:
It's precisely by avoiding the temptation to create a centralized multicultural department with huge power that David Crombie does all Canadians a big
favour.
I really stand behind this quote.
I know it is very important for my colleagues across the way to have this department separate, but it is not in the best interests of the Canadian people to do so. As I said at the beginning, and I do not want to repeat myself but it is very important that I say it in both official languages, as an immigrant, I do not feel that I am inferior or superior to anyone in Canada. I want to be equal.
I am so proud to have the privilege of staying in Canada that I do not ask for any special favours. Many, many people try to do that but I do not want any special favours. I want to be equal.
A separate department would, in my view, risk the development of a kind of a ghetto and would give encouragement to a view that multiculturalism is not an integral element of our whole society but rather some form of add-on or special program.

Madam Speaker, I recently attended a seminar in Montreal, and I would like to share that experience with the House, knowing that my colleague, the Hon. Member for Bourassa (Mr. Rossi) is going to listen closely, as well as the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi), because this involves my community. I attended a seminar and someone pointed out to me the need of developing special programs for the visible minorities. One visible minority put some kind of a proposal to me, suggesting: We want to have a special program for us

March 15, 1988
Canadian Multiculturalism Act
blacks as a visible minority, because we want to have a chance as Italians had in Canada.
For example, would the condition of multiculturalism with respect to health matters or employment strategies or small business be more valuable for Canada? Multiculturalism should not be put in a corner. It must be reflected in every way the federal Government works. This commitment is a lot more than words. It reflects this Government's record and demonstrates our resolve.
The record is clear. First, we must tell the House about our good record. Our hon. friends never mention that. I do not blame them. They are in the opposition, they are not interested in the truth. They are not interested in saying something good about this Government. No one is perfect, but at least we have something good. This Government established a Standing Committee on Multiculturalism. We promised it, we have it, and my two friends are on it. They can speak freely and put their views. It is good for all of us. No one did it before. We are the first.
Thank you.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
You are there. I know you are having a lot of fun. You work hard, but you must say that we did it. You did not do it.
We introduced the Employment Equity Act. We convened the first national conference on policy and urban municipalities. We increased significantly the number of appointments made to federal boards and commissions. I wish I could give all the names but I do not think we have the time.
Table it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
We can table any names and we can say that we did a lot of things. I will give some names but I will not have time to give them all.
The other day we received a letter from the National Congress of Italian Canadians, an organization which I know well. The Congress congratulated the Government of Canada for introducing a Bill that will formally recognize the multicultural reality of Canada through the first national multiculturalism Act. I must say that I will not read the whole letter but there is another paragraph that criticizes something. It is not perfect. It looks as though my hon. friend from York West wrote the letter for them.
No.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Yes. Let me read you another paragraph that you will like because it is negative. The Congress, while appreciating the value of the initiative, is concerned that some
of the key elements proposed by the various cultural communities and recommended by the Standing Committee on Multiculturalism have not been incorporated in the Bill.
Right on.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Of course. They did not come to us, they listened to you. You are preaching these words. If I go on I will see some phrases which my friend used a few moments ago in his speech. Maybe they listen to you but maybe they should listen to us, too, because we have something positive to say. Well, maybe my hon. colleague does not agree with us.

Madam Speaker, the Minister quoted from many sources this morning to show that we had the support of all the newspapers, and rightly so. After the Bill on multiculturalism was tabled on December 1, the Toronto Star came out strongly in favour of the Bill. The Secretary of State has already told the House about the reasons given by the newspaper.
This newspaper was quoted many times this morning because, as you know, Madam Speaker, the Toronto Star is supposed to be the most neutral newspaper in Canada. To my knowledge, it is not a Conservative newspaper. Everyone says so, which means that no one can accuse us of partisanship.
I would like to quote another article published in the Toronto Star:
"It is precisely by avoiding the temptation to create a centralized multiculturalism department with huge powers that David Crombie does all Canadians a big favour. Rather than shove ethnic groups into permanent multicultural ghettos, he is content to have all Canadians treated the same when it comes to protecting their basic rights and freedoms".
I like this article, Madam Speaker, and I intend to keep it as it summarizes all the questions of the two Hon. Members opposite as well as the concerns of our national Congress, which I know quite well and for which I have a lot of respect, and of the Italian community throughout Canada. It is true that these people are concerned, but perhaps they should have consulted us more to know what we had in mind and why we did certain things. The Government always has reasons for acting as it does.
We are always willing to listen. We are always willing to hear what people have to say. When we travel around this country, Madam Speaker, it is surprising to find that every community has something to say. Every piece of the mosaic has its own views, and we have to respect them.
On several occasions, I heard people talking. We would never want to see a ghetto! We would never want to be separated from the others! We want to be together to build this country. That is what I always thought, Madam Speaker, even if when the committee started meeting some years ago, I was seriously considering this issue. But after having consulted and talked things over, although nobody told me to change my
March 15, 1988

mind, I learned that there are realities in this country which must be respected.
Madam Speaker, I can only agree and I am sure that most Hon. Members support the way multiculturalism operates in this country.
The commitment to preserve and enhance multiculturalism in Canada cannot remain only a vague promise. It requires an effort to educate people and make them aware of the intercultural reality. It requires that we put to effective use the talents, trade skills and cultural understanding of Canadian citizens who have roots in other countries of the world. This commitment requires also that we strenghen Canadian unity and that we seek to increase communication and exchanges with other parts of the world.
While addressing the Canadian association of the multilingual press last October, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) was right when he made the following statement:
The Canadian Multiculturalism Act will help shape our country's vision and
steer our future development as a unique and dynamic country which knows
how to benefit from the experience and talents of Canadians who emigrated
from the four corners of the world.
When I hear "from the four corners of the world", Madam Speaker, I see myself in the picture.
I am sure I am not the only one who feels that we must take advantage of these resources. I refer to the talents and experience of our very diversified multilingual and multiracial population, as well as the ability of our institutional resources, to make of multiculturalism a dynamic new force in the so-called "global village".
Famous Quebec sociologist Raymond Breton noted that as long as a group sees that some of its members are not integrated in its own government machinery it cannot feel it fully belongs to its new country. The participation of representatives from all cultural groups to the policy planning and decision making process of the federal Government is of utmost importance at a time when we are seeking to promote multiculturalism in Canada as a whole.
I am proud to say the Progressive Conservative Government has made significant progress in this field. There has been a considerable increase in the number of ethnic group members appointed to federal councils, commissions and organizations. Earlier my colleague was urging me to name a few. I will single out just a few, Mr. Speaker, because I do not have time to read the whole impressive list.
Our Government sought faithfully to reflect Canada's multicultural reality through these appointments: Joseph Picinninni to the Citizenship Court; Berverley Oda to the CRTC; Emerson Mascoll to the CN board of directors; Wally Majesky to the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation board of directors; Cesar de Morias to the Immigration Appeal Board; Roman Senkiw to the board of the Canadian Commercial Corporation; Irene Chu to the Immigration Appeal Board;
Canadian Multiculturalism Act
and Con Di Nino as President of the Harbourfront Corporation.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I want to repeat what I have been telling my fellow Canadians and my Multiculturalism Canada colleagues: Multiculturalism is not only for the Italians, it is not only for the Greeks, it is not only for the Chinese, multiculturalism is a sign of harmony, it holds this country together and united. This morning our Minister aptly summed it up in three words, and I want to conclude my remarks by repeating those three words: liberty, stability, and opportunity.

Mr. Speaker, although the Member who just spoke obviously brings passion and sincerity to the debate today as he did to his work before becoming a Member of Parliament, it is sad that in his capacity as Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Multiculturalism he has made, on a number of occasions, very loosey-goosey, offensive statements which I would like him to address.
However, before I ask him to do that, I would like to question him about his statements on the evolution of the mutliculturalism policy in this country. He asks why we had not done this and why we had not done that. One can follow that line of questioning to the ends of the earth. The Parliamentary Secretary fails to recognize that there has been an evolution of sorts in the Multiculturalism Directorate from 1971, when it was made an official policy of governments, to the present day.
The Member fails to see that when his Government assumed power in 1984, instead of propelling that policy into the future boldly and progressively it basically legislated in 1988 values and principles which were not new but were born and raised in the 1960s and 1970s. This indicates that the Conservative Party which forms the Government of today has failed miserably to be creative and define the second phase. In its failure to define the second phase it is left with an embracing of the principles and structures of the past. Therefore, for the Conservative Party the future of multiculturalism is in the past.
We say that, more important than debating what has happened until now, is to focus our energy, thoughts, and creativity on the present and the future. If the future policy lives in the past, it will become irrelevant. I am sure that no one in this House wants that to happen. I think the Parliamentary Secretary fails to grasp that. He prefers to dilly-dally in what happened in the sixties and seventies. Let us look at the nineties and beyond and ask ourselves as a collectivity in Parliament how to form a policy which will meet the aspirations of today and the future rather than simply deal with the past.
The Parliamentary Secretary said that people in this country do not recognize that it is a privilege to be here and that if they

March 15, 1988
Canadian Multiculturism Act
do not do so they are not decent and good Canadians. He also made reference to people in this country who want special favours. I believe those are very suggestive terms, to say the least. To whom was the Member referring when he said that people in this country do not recognize the greatness of this country? Who in this country is looking for special favours? I have found no one who is.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to begin with the very important question which the Member asked at the end of his remarks. My colleague misunderstood me. I am going to read the "blues" to see whether he is right or wrong, but I would like to clear up the error.
I said it was a privilege for me to be in this country as it is for many citizens who arrive here, and that I hope they recognize that. I did not make the suggestion which the Hon. Member says I did. I said that I hope they realize that and if they do not realize that it is time that they did. I said that if they do not realize that this country is the best country in the world, they are not good Canadians. However, I have never met anyone who has indicated to me that they do not realize that this is a beautiful country. That is what I meant, and I do not want the Member to change my words. I said as well that I thank Canada for giving me this privilege.
On December 1, when speaking on the multiculturalism Bill in this House, I said that it was a privilege, not only for ethnic groups, but for all Canadians. I still say that everyone should be involved in multiculturalism because when people look at their ancestry they realize that their ancestors all came from elsewhere. I am proud to be part of that.

Mr. Speaker, let me make this perfectly clear. Anyone who cares to do a modicum of research will discover that the origin of all Canadians goes much further back. Everyone should say: Multiculturalism is not only for Quebecers or for Canadians born in this country, it is for everybody, for where do our ancestors come from? Even Adam and Eve ...

My colleague says that he does not like me to speak about the past. I do not blame him because his Party did not do much in the past. I mentioned earlier that Bill C-48 did not recognize what this multiculturalism Bill recognizes. The Member says that I am in the sixties and seventies and that he wants to be in the nineties. This Bill goes to the year 2000 and 1 am proud of that.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: There are two minutes left in the period for quesions and comments. The Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Epp).

Mr. Speaker, it is always good to have a minute or two saved for one. I will be brief. The Member for Duvernay (Mr. Della Noce) is as energetic a Parliamentary Secretary as we have. He is doing a good job here today. He is also an honest man.
In bringing forward the letter fom the National Congress of Italian Canadians he has done us a service. He read a sentence and then, under a little urging from us, provided an additional sentence. He suggested that the National Congress of Italian Canadians is critical of this Bill because they listened to a certain person. I think he meant it was the Member for York West (Mr. Marchi), and I see political partisan jealousies there, unless he meant that they were listening to me as well.
I would worry if he thinks that the opposition critics, one or both, are convincing these organizations of what they should say. I assume he had something to do with the development of the Bill into the form in which it is before us now, this half loaf that we have been given.
Why was the Government not more responsive to the Canadian Ethnocultural Council and these national organizations, the majority of which wanted some sort of institutional development beyond the status quo we now have? If they did not want a department, many of them saw the validity of a commissioner. Why rejection of both?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are faced with a time factor problem which would be very interesting . . . but still 1 want to congratulate my honourable colleague because I know that he is interested in the cause, and we had the pleasure to sit together on the Committee on Multiculturalism. The letter, a little earlier ... Yes, he is right, I have it here. Quotations should always be avoided because as is often seen during Ora! Question Period we tend to quote anything that supports our point of view while ignoring anything else that goes against it.
I would be glad to give him a copy. He is right to commend us on principle. And I believe that on principle everybody should commend us, even the groups that speak up. Because it still is a premiere, not only in Canada, but a world premiere and we should be proud of it. Since I don't have the time to read the whole letter, if my honourable colleague wants me to send him a copy, I will be glad to do so.
I also want to say that there certainly were many requests. Eight or nine 1 believe were addressed to the Committee. But it must be understood that there are not always convincing reasons to support all sorts of arguments. It is certain that we could have given some to explain why not everything has been done. But when there are convincing arguments, should we give in every time to the request? I referred to what my colleague's party which formed the previous Government had done with Bill C-48, where there was no recognition . . .

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:

Mir. However, my colleague from Duvernay said that some groups have apparently asked him for special favours. Since the member from York West spoke in English, I am repeating it in good French Canadian.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I fully understood the question, and I said that one day we had invited ethnic groups to attend a Tory symposium and we dealt briefly with that Bill. Several made a report but unfortunately a group said: We want a special grant because we are a visible minority.
