Mr. Speaker, on March 7 I asked a question of the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin) about a remission order that had been granted to Goodyear Tire Company worth $50 million over four years. I asked whether the Minister was prepared to rescind that order in light of the fact that company officials
March 15, 1988

had subsequently stated that they would have made some improvements that were carried out without the benefit of that remission order. If the Hon. Minister was not prepared to do that, I asked if he would at least tell us what guarantees were in place to assure the Canadian taxpayers that a benefit equal to the $50 million would be there for the Canadian people. Those two questions could have been answered either yes or no, with or without an explanation. In fact, the answer was that I was told that I was wrong. That to me, Mr. Speaker, was a non sequitur.
Was I wrong, Mr. Speaker, on March 4, 1987 when I went with the 1,574 Goodyear workers in my riding who lost their jobs at Goodyear and we demonstrated at the head office of Goodyear, and I made a commitment to them? I stated that if Goodyear would grant transfer rights to those workers to any new plant that would be built, then I would move heaven and earth to see that any form of federal financial assistance was there to ensure that that new world class tire plant was developed. On the other hand, if Goodyear would not grant those transfer rights I stated that I would equally move heaven and earth to ensure that not a single cent of federal tax money was ever spent on or for the benefit of Goodyear. Was I wrong to make that commitment? In the absence of Goodyear giving that, and it never did give that commitment for transfer rights, what we had was transition at taxpayers' cost and at the cost of those individual workers who lost their jobs and who were told that if anything ever happened again for Goodyear, they could go and line up like other workers for new jobs that might come along.
In that same year, on December 20, by Order in Council the Government that I seek to support made this benefit for Goodyear. At the time I called it a cruel joke. Was I wrong to call it that? An Order in Council is a secret approach to public business. In the course of things, it is not something that gets debated on the floor of the House of Commons. If it had not been for the assiduous work of Canadian Press reporter Gordon McIntosh, who went through a stack of Orders in Council and come out on January 8 with the evidence that, lo and behold, two days before Christmas the Government had given this undeserved Christmas present to Goodyear then, as the Member of Parliament most directly affected, I probably would not even have known about it.
The issue here is not the use of remission orders, it is the abuse of remission orders. If parliamentary reform is to mean anything, it must mean that Members of Parliament have an opportunity to be here in the House of Commons and bring to bear on the issues in this country their knowledge, experience, and the views of their constituents.
Before I entered this House on February 24, 1984, I wrote an article on Government and corporate bail-outs. I pointed out that corporate bail-outs were nothing new in Canada. Canadians had grown accustomed to private enterprise at public expense. I went on and talked about the need for a clear policy framework for this type of Government subvention to the private sector. I even concluded with the comment that
Adjournment Debate
failure to have a coherent bail-out policy can lead to some Alice in Wonderland like results. Little did I think that Alice in Wonderland would be visited on Etobicoke-Lakeshore, but most assuredly it was.
Was it wrong for me to write to the President of Goodyear about this remission order and point out unequivocally my views, and for him to respond on January 18 and state that he appreciated the frankness of my views? He added that the federal Government has recognized the need to revitalize Canada's tire industry by encouraging new investments. He said as he understands it, this is the purpose of duty remission. The letter was signed Scott H. Busby, President, Good Year Canada Inc.
If that was the purpose of the remission order, then why should it have applied to Goodyear? Goodyear has two tire plants left in this country, one at Medicine Hat, Alberta, with some 250 employees. There it makes bias ply tires. Goodyear has a little niche in the market that is shrinking. The success and the longevity will depend entirely upon market forces, and no amount of government bail-outs will add or subtract to the jobs or the production there. The second, and only other tire plant that Goodyear has in this country, is at Valleyfield, Quebec. It is a new and modern plant. It was built after General Motors put in its plant at Ste. Therese. It is tied selling. Goodyear has its market for radial tires at GM, Ste. Therese. Last year the Government gave a $210 million benefit to GM at Ste. Therese. There is little likelihood in my mind that there will be any jeopardy to the Goodyear production at Valleyfield. That is a given. That is secure.
What was the basis, what was the need for this benefit to be conferred on Goodyear? Bearing in mind that the Financial Administration Act provides for remission orders where there are anomalies and unjust results, corrective measures can be taken under Section 17 and remission orders provided. It is not the place to enact industrial policy for this country. Remission orders are hip pocket, ad hoc measures to deal with something and they are being used for industrial policy. If the Government believes that there should be something in this area, let it bring on to the floor of the House of Commons something called the tire industry manufacturers assistance act, 1988 and let Members of Parliament who have these plants in their ridings and know something about the issues deal with it.
When I dealt with the officials and tried to get some explanation about the abuse, Mr. Speaker, I felt that I was seeing an episode of Yes, Minister that had been jointly scripted by Franz Kafka and George Orwell.

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre H. Vincent (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
If I may, Mr. Speaker, I should like first of all to point out to the Hon. Member that the remission order granted to the Goodyear Tire Company is worth $25 million over a four-year period, and not $50 million as he has

March 15, 1988
Adjournment Debate
just stated. I should like also to emphasize that these $25 million are not a subsidy, but a remission on duties otherwise payable on this company's future imports.
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the Hon. Member is aware that the Canadian tire industry is making a major contribution to the economy of this country, with a production worth up to $1.7 billion in 1985. Tire manufacturing in Canada provide jobs to some 11,000 people, including 4,300 in Ontario, 4,000 in Nova Scotia, and 2,700 in Quebec. This industry has been exposed to strong restructuring pressures, to a series of takeovers, mergers and acquisitions which have resulted in a significant number of job lossses. Moreover, in anticipation of free trade with the United States, it is important, not to say essential, that the Canadian tire industry should become completely competitive on the North American market.
A remission is considered as a proper mechanism to encourage new investments in Canadian tire manufacturing firms and thus ensure the future of that industry in Canada. More specifically, the purpose of this remission of duty is to help tire makers streamline their facilities and rationalize their North American operations. Moreover, the tire duty remission program will avert future job losses and, as you know, will preserve existing jobs in this industry.
Clearly, if tire makers do not meet the expectations both of the Government and the industry, it will be the Government's responsibility to put an end to these benefits.
The Government is quite concerned about the effects of manpower upheaval and disruption from lay-offs. However, we should not loose sight of the jobs which will be secured as a result to the steps taken by the Government. I understand that only a few workers have been laid off and could still be recalled following the closing of the Goodyear plant in Toronto. I understand also that Goodyear has set up an employment priority program in Valleyfield and Medicine Hat. I know that the company has offered the same transfer rights to any new plant which could be built within the next five years, provided such employees meet the hiring requirements.
I have also been advised that Goodyear not only has met all of its legal commitments, but exceeded its obligations under the agreement it signed with its employees, when it ended its operations.
Mr. Speaker, our Government feels that the tire duty remission program will help tire manufacturers become more efficient. It is quite concerned about the long term profitability of Canadian tire manufacturers and we believe that the steps we have taken will open for them interesting opportunities in the future.

HAZARDOUS SUBSTANCES-PRESENCE OF DIOXIN IN PAPER PRODUCTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, last week was my birthday. In fact, it was on March 11, to be exact.

subtopic: HAZARDOUS SUBSTANCES-PRESENCE OF DIOXIN IN PAPER PRODUCTS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: HAZARDOUS SUBSTANCES-PRESENCE OF DIOXIN IN PAPER PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Thank you all very much for those kind acknowledgements and applause. But no, Mr. Speaker, there is certainly no need for you to sing Happy Birthday tonight. Do not worry about the cake because I was well looked after. I had a birthday cake here in Ottawa with which my staff very kindly provided me and I had a cake back home as well. Do not worry about that.
No, Mr. Speaker, I will not tell you how old I am. However, I will tell you that I am so old that when I was a kid, I used to get handkerchiefs as birthday presents. You remember what handkerchiefs are, do you not, Mr. Speaker? Those were the things we used to use before there were those paper tissues that we use now to wipe our noses with. Does that ring a bell?
I used to get handkerchiefs for every birthday and every Christmas. They came in all sorts of sizes and colours. Most of them, of course, were white, and the best kind were made of Irish linen. There were all sorts of other kinds as well and lots of pretty colours. I suppose they were supposed to be colour coordinated, but I did not understand that in those days.
Shortly after the Second World War, I got an awful lot of khaki handkerchiefs. I think they were probably war-surplus handkerchiefs. Then I used to get lovely handkerchiefs with my initials on them, the real fancy kind.
I have collected so many handkerchiefs over this period of time that I have a huge drawer full of them at home, and I never use one of them. The reason of course for that is that we do not use handkerchiefs any longer to any real extent, we use these paper tissues.
When I first started using paper tissues, we called them Kleenex. They were soft, strong and they popped up in the box. That was the only kind of paper tissue available, but now just about every paper company makes a paper tissue like that.
I am very seriously considering going back to using my old handkerchiefs again. This is because they have discovered small amounts of something called dioxin in these paper tissues and not only in paper tissues but in paper towels, coffee filters and paper plates. The levels of the dioxin appear to be small, but in fact they have been found to be higher in paper tissues and in paper towels than in some other things. Dioxin is an extremely toxic substance. Trace or small amounts have been known to cause birth defects, cancer and damage to the immune system.
The pulp and paper industry tells us that it suspects that these dioxins in paper tissues are formed by the chlorine-
*1%
;||
March 15, 1988

bleaching process that is used in the paper-making here in Canada and the United States. In Europe, they use an oxygen-bleaching process and they apparently do not have the same dioxin problem. Of course, the industry says that low levels of dioxin pose no real and immediate threat or health hazard to us, but you will recall that a toxicologist with the environmental defense fund in the U.S. said these are products from which we can assume there will be a transfer of dioxins into ourselves.
In January of this year dioxin was found in the waters near the MacMillan Bloedel Harmac pulp mill in Nanaimo, British Columbia. You know where that is, Mr. Speaker. It is not very far from Victoria, as you well know. A spokesman for the federal Department of Fisheries and Oceans said at that time it should not come as any great surprise to anyone that there was dioxin found in the waters near that pulp mill. It may not be a great surprise but it is a matter of great concern. That is why I am asking the Parliamentary Secretary what in the heck we are going to do about it. What action is he and his Minister going to take to make sure this health hazard is eliminated?
Are we going to follow the European method and use an oxygen bleaching process to eliminate dioxin from paper products? Are we at least going to warn people that there is this problem with things like paper tissues? If we do not do something pretty soon, I am going to have to go back to putting handkerchiefs on my shopping list for Christmas and birthdays. What about it, Mr. Parliamentary Secretary? What are we going to do?

speakeroldname: Mr. Blaine A. Thacker (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: HAZARDOUS SUBSTANCES-PRESENCE OF DIOXIN IN PAPER PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to respond with further details to the question raised by the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Redway) regarding the steps being taken by this Government to protect the health of Canadians from the effects of dioxins and furans in paper products.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) has already informed the House that in early October, 1987, he commissioned an interdepartmental committee with representatives from Health and Welfare Canada, Environment Canada and Consumer and Corporate Affairs Canada. This committee has met several times to co-ordinate the activities under way within the three departments and to ensure there is effective communication among the various groups working on this issue.
Within National Health and Welfare a task force of experts from the Health Protection Branch has met to review the preliminary data reported to the media in late September by the American Paper Institute, API, and by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, EPA. Although both American groups had hoped to have their final reports available for release in November, the necessity of ensuring these extremely complex analyses for dioxins and furans at such low levels are accurate and reproducible, resulted in an unavoidable delay.
Adjournment Debate
The EPA has now released details of its kraft pulp paper mill study. The API has provided a descriptive report of its research work on the migration of dioxins and furans from paper products to contact foods and has issued its assessment of the health risk associated with human exposure in contact paper products such as diapers, tissues and bond papers. It should be emphasized that it has taken nearly three years to complete the arduous task of developing the capability to sample and analyse these products, pulps, sludges and waste waters.
Officials within the Health Protection Branch have been able to complete an assessment of available data and have concluded that the minute concentrations of dioxins and furans found in some bleached paper products are well below the level of concern for human health. A quantitative risk assessment will be carried out using data currently being developed by contractors to the API and by Health and Welfare Canada laboratories.
National Health and Welfare does not expect to complete in a few months what has taken others almost two years to carry out. This research is technically extremely difficult and costly. Nevertheless, Canada has earned a reputation as a world leader in dioxin and furan research, and is fully capable of assessing the need for further analytical data and providing the technical skill to obtain it. Assessment of the implications of such data is also complex. However, it will be completed promptly once the data under development are released.
Work is also under way in the Department of the Environment, which has the responsibility for developing appropriate control strategies for the pulp and paper industry. Department of Environment officials have set up a Canadian task force to investigate the levels of dioxin and furan releases from pulp and paper manufacturing and, as appropriate, to investigate control strategies for the industry. The task force, in connection with the provinces and industry, will implement a sampling program and make appropriate recommendations on control needs for the industry.
Officials in both departments are in direct contact with industry in Canada and the U.S. to ensure that research on this issue is properly focused and complementary. It is in the best interests of Canadians that we build on all available and reliable data rather than ignoring those studies carried out by non-governmental groups.
These are the steps being taken by the Government to ensure that paper products sold in Canada pose no adverse health risk to Canadians and to ensure that sources of dioxins and furans in Canada be identified and controlled. I think I can safely say to my hon. colleague that he can continue to use paper tissue products without fear.

Adjournment Debate
EL SALVADOR-UNION WORKERS FIRED UPON BY MILITARY/ BOMBING OF OSCAR ROMERO COMMITTEE OFFICE

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 2, I asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) a question about human rights violations in El Salvador in relation to Canada's support for the Government of El Salvador. In particular, I referred to a report which I had sent him the previous day that the United Workers of El Salvador, when demonstrating peacefully for the release of hundreds of political prisoners illegally held in Mariona Prison, were fired upon by the military which seriously wounded the Secretary-General of the union, Julio Portillo. I asked the Minister to request the Duarte Government to account for this violence and for the growing attacks during the last few months by the Duarte Government against trade unionists.
At the same time I asked the Minister to take up the matter of the bombing on the same day of the office of the Oscar Romero Committee of Mothers for the Detained and Disappeared. Two mothers were wounded and their files were all destroyed. The next day the Minister of National Defence threatened to break up their weekly peaceful marches if they continued to ask for news of their husbands, brothers, and sons who had disappeared. The Minister promised to answer. Nine and one-half months later he has not yet answered me.
The Canadian Government is renewing its bilateral aid to El Salvador although the Government ended that aid in 1984 on account of human rights violations which threatened basic civil and political society in that country. The present Government reinstituted bilateral aid on the explicit premise that the Duarte Government had both the will and the capacity to bring about peace and respect for basic human rights as well as judicial, economic, and social reform.
We should note that bilateral aid is not the only form in which aid can be given. It can also be given through Canadian non-governmental organizations and through multilateral institutions which can do it just as well as can the Canadian Government. Choosing to do it bilaterally sends a signal to the El Salvadoran Government and the rest of the world that our Government supports the Government of El Salvador and approves and accepts the Duarte regime as a regime worth working through. It in fact claims that the Duarte regime is improving and trying to continue to improve the human rights situation there.
The facts are the opposite. Since the time I spoke, political violence has remained at a very high level and, in fact, is increasing in El Salvador according to all independent observers. The total body count might be down, but that only reflects a decision on the part of the death squads to target the leadership of human rights organizations, trade unions, cooperatives, and other progressive groups.
The murder of Herbert Ernesto Anaya, the President of the Salvadoran Non-governmental Human Rights Commission on October 26 brought the whole question of human rights back into world attention. The Council on Hemispheric Affairs, in
its Human Rights Review from 1987, once again named El Salvador as among the worst violators of human rights in the hemisphere.
The United Nations Sub-Commission on the Prevention of Discrimination and Protection of Minorities reported on September 2, last year, that:
... serious and massive violations of human rights are still occurring in El Salvador.
As I said, the body count is only one indication of the human rights situation in El Salvador. A better one is the number of military officers prosecuted for human rights violations. That number is zero.
The only part of the Esquipulas peace accord that appears to be honoured by the Salvadoran government was the amnesty they provided to the death squads who killed trade unionists and other critics of the status quo.
The U.S. based lawyers Committee for Human Rights in El Salvador testified last year that:
The collapse of El Salvador's criminal justice system is general and pervasive. Indeed, as best as we can tell, that system has never functioned effectively in the criminal justice field.
Land reform, a key issue in El Salvador, as in most Central American countries, is failing. Duarte's land reform program has turned into a shallow farce, overseen exclusively by organizations supporting the Government. At least 19 legally recognized peasant organizations have been excluded from participation.
The most authoritative human rights non-governmental organization in Canada monitoring latin American concerns is the Inter-Church Committee on Human Rights in Latin America. It represents most of the major denominations in Canada and conducts both on-site visits and continual assessments of reports and documentation.
In their most recent report on El Salvador, they quote our Government's reply to the Report of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade, in which our Government said:
... the degree to which human rights are respected is a factor in determining eligibility for Canadian development assistance.
Well, to quote the Inter-Church Committee:
In view of their careful assessment of the over-all human rights situation prevailing in El Salvador during 1987, the churches and church bodies which make up the Inter-Church Committee on Human Rights in Latin America believe, in accordance with the above stated policy of the Canadian Government, that there should be no new bilateral Canadian aid given the Government of El Salvador under present conditions.
I call on the Government to end bilateral aid to the murderous government of Duarte in El Salvador.

March 15, 1988

had any knowledge of the wounding of Julio Portillo, an official of the United Workers of El Salvador. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) replied that enquiries would be made into the case.
Our embassy has now confirmed that Mr. Portillo was shot on May 31, during a protest outside Mariona Prison. Fortunately, we understand he is recovering. There conflicting versions of what happened. One version is that he was shot by soldiers during a scuffle to remove protest placards. A second version is that he was shot by prison guards as the protesters were walking away from the site. A third version is that the protestors themselves fired the shot, accidentally wounding Mr. Portillo.
The Hon. Member also requested that inquiries be made into the bombing of the offices of the Oscar Romero Committee of Mothers for the Detained and Disappeared. Our embassy confirms that a bomb exploded in those offices on may 28 injuring two members. To date no one has claimed responsibility.
Adjournment Debate
The Canadian Government deplores the incidents of violence that continue in El Salvador perpetrated by both sides in the conflict. As we have in the past, we will continue to urge further reform at every opportunity both bilaterally and multilaterally. Inquiries on specific cases such as these also serve to register official Canadian interest and concern.
The latest incident that has come to our attention concerning the United Workers of El Salvador is the arrest and beating of labour leader Umberto Centeno on March 10. Although he was subsequently released, our embassy in San Jose, Costa Rica, is investigating the incident.
